The chromatic dispersion exhibited in this submarine fiber differs significantly from that of standard telecommunication fibers. We demonstrate that direct detection (DD) offers a viable solution for such field-trial backhaul applications, yielding a bit-error-rate (BBR) optimized distance of 60 km. Furthermore, DD proves effective in mitigating coherent crosstalk and cyclic cross-phase modulation interference within the system. When evaluating DD performance against a reference link using coherent detection with digital signal processing, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of receiver sensitivity and optical signal SNR. Additional tests included varying filter combinations, offset frequencies, and oscillatory SNR paths to assess DD tolerance to chromatic dispersion. Notably, the system's dispersion tolerance is influenced by the preamble length of the multi-bit lock-in amplifier. Although DD offers lower sensitivity, it eliminates the need for expensive digital signal processing and optical signal regeneration equipment, making it an ideal solution for South-East Asian submarine backhaul routes where amplifier noise is dominant and dispersion values are moderate. The study concludes that DD is a practical and cost-effective technique for optimizing spectral and time-domain BBRs up to 100 km and 56 Gbit/s, respectively, within South-East Asian backhaul scenarios. This research provides a roadmap for deploying DD in South-East Asian optical backbones, where moderate chromatic dispersion and preamble-length-induced cyclic interference are the primary concerns. We suggest implementing DD-based BBR optimization alongside simple pilot-assisted carrier-phase estimation and DD for achieving higher spectral efficiencies (up to 215 Gbit/s) in regional optical backhaul over uncompensated submarine fiber. Current cost-efficiency calculations indicate that DD can reduce the total system expense by 27% compared to the reference system.
Over the last few years, optimizing the joint design of repeater spacing and data rates has been crucial for maximizing the transmission distance of existing optical fibers without incurring excessive costs. Typically, machine learning (ML) algorithms are employed to simulate non-linear fiber dynamics in optical waveform optimization for coherent detection. However, in optical systems utilizing direct detection (DD), ML-based simulation of self-phase modulation (SPM) is unnecessary and can actually hinder error-rate optimization. We propose using DD to manage SPM-induced distortions, which can be adjusted via changes in repeater spacing. This approach was validated in a direct-current (DC) based laboratory trial. We introduce an automatic dilation optimizer that reframes this challenge as weight pruning along the time axis, enabling the simultaneous training of thousands of tailored TCN variants within a single network. Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are potent tools for classifying unaligned temporal data, their extensive hyperparameter space hinders automatic specialization for specific time series. We propose TimeBlock, a novel architecture designed to streamline the creation of end-to-end trainable, efficient CNN models for unaligned time series classification. TimeBlock offers a SPARSE hyperparameter landscape that allows for rapid optimization via performance-based hyperparameter search, yielding a 1.3 performance gain over the next best competing architecture when optimized within 50 minutes. Additionally, TimeBlock achieves a 2.7 training time advantage over GridSearch when latterly optimized and supports fully end-to-end learning. The source code can be found at https://github.com/andrewjstevens/TimeBlock.

We present a method for automatically learning the hyperparameters of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) used in heartbeat classification. Our approach formulates hyperparameter optimization as a sequence modeling task, leveraging a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) to learn a mapping from heart signal statistics to hyperparameters. Specifically, the ALBA algorithm, which is parametric for each (D)LE, efficiently determines the first-order correspondents of (D)LE-inductive formulas. We introduce an algorithm that utilizes ALBA's rules and algebraic framework to reverse its steps within the DLE context, thereby effectively calculating an inductive formula's correspondent in first-order logic. This approach generalizes recent methods developed by Daniel per Sahlqvist and Alexander N. Kuznetsov for propositional distributive and Boolean lattice expansions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the algorithm's application to specific cases in predicate logic, including discrete and dense linear orders, affine lattices, and Boolean algebras. Our results illustrate that ALBA's computational efficiency extends to first-order correspondence, offering significant advantages for tasks such as query evaluation. The proposed algorithm serves as a practical instrument for researchers in DLEs to identify inductive formulas and their correspondents across various logical systems with appropriate lattice components. These findings also provide actionable insights for logicians seeking to prove canonicity without relying on ALBA. To support future work on first-order query evaluation, we present the "corpus" of inductive formulas and their correspondents generated by this algorithm. As part of the special issue on "Query Evaluation for Non-Classical Logics," this work aims to advance the utilization of ALBA in canonicity proof generation and query evaluation. This paper examines whether the ALBA algorithm can determine the first-order correspondent of arbitrary first-order formulas involving basic connectives, relations, and arbitrary quantifiers. While ALBA was originally designed for modal and lattice-based logics, its modular nature suggests a broader applicability. Although a general solution remains unattained, we successfully solve the problem for specific signature extensions, such as prelinear and continuous lattices. Consequently, we establish a method for ensuring canonicity in first-order logic formulas across these signatures. While the conventional stance holds that table instances must adhere to all imposed functional dependencies, this view fails to account for the increasing difficulty of guaranteeing instance consistency when dependencies are meant to represent implicit knowledge about real-world data. Conversely, merging tables via natural joins often becomes impossible or yields an incomplete result if every table instance is required to satisfy all functional dependencies. To address these challenges, we introduce a more pragmatic method for handling inconsistencies in tables with nulls and functional dependencies, which is particularly relevant for data integration and preprocessing.

In this approach, functional dependencies are categorized into two groups: those whose instance compliance is mandatory and those that are optional. For optional dependencies, we define a satisfaction degree that quantifies how consistently the data aligns with the dependency. Consequently, inconsistent instances of optional dependencies can be repaired by substituting null values; the cost of such repairs is directly proportional to the degree of inconsistency. We formulate the conversion of an entire table to satisfy a specific functional dependency as a constraint satisfaction problem, applicable whether the table contains no nulls or contains only nulls. Additionally, we extend this method to scenarios involving partial fixed values.

The consequences of this extension include a proof that, in tables without fixed values or with fully fixed rows, a maximal consistent extension exists that satisfies all optional functional dependencies. However, this result does not hold when fixed rows are involved. Furthermore, we examine the complexity of finding a maximal consistent extension for general tables with nulls and optional dependencies, alongside the related issue of minimizing repair costs. Finally, we demonstrate how this framework can be leveraged to define similarity measures for tables. This paper extends the findings presented in [8].

This work aims to resolve inconsistencies in tables featuring missing values and functional dependencies, a critical factor in merging such tables. We define a consistent table as one where every table instance satisfies all specified functional dependencies, which is a standard definition for tables without missing values. However, enforcing strict compliance with all dependencies in tables with nulls can lead to overly restrictive conditions, potentially resulting in an inconsistent table if any single instance violates a dependency, or worse, a maximally inconsistent table if repairs are solely limited to modifying null values.

To manage these inconsistencies, we propose a solution where functional dependencies are divided into core and auxiliary sets. Core dependencies must be satisfied by all table instances, whereas auxiliary dependencies offer flexibility; their consistency is optional, and any inconsistency is quantified by a weight. Designed for object manipulation, this approach enables the repetition of a demonstrated task on new instances within the same category by optimizing for a pose whose descriptor matches the observed demonstration. We present Instance-to-Template (I2T) translation, a new approach for 6-DoF object detection that infers object presence and pose from a single 2D image by optimizing a transformation that maps a point-cloud instance to a canonical template. Unlike previous methods that depend on 2D-image-based descriptors suffering from perspective aliasing, or those that require full instance point clouds often lacking in monocular systems, our instance-centric I2T method utilizes a partial point cloud of the object. Our results show that I2T achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) 6-DoF object detection on the real-world ACAD (Additive Manufacturing Cell Assembly Demonstration) dataset while requiring 10x less memory than SOTA solutions. This technique is particularly valuable for detecting object orientations with 3-DoF freedom (roll, pitch, yaw) when only a subset of the object is visible in an image. We provide a thorough ablation study and analysis of the I2T method's point-wise performance.

We introduce a straightforward approach for 6-DoF pose estimation that employs a single instance mesh and its corresponding 2D descriptor. This method identifies a Global Optimal Template (GOT) for each object instance that is easy to align with a model. Such alignment allows for the efficient estimation of all 6 degrees of freedom using a neural descriptor network. In contrast to previous techniques that rely on 2D descriptors alone—which lead to ambiguous pose estimates when significant instance variation exists—our solution offers several advantages: it requires minimal memory compared to other SOTA methods

Our study examines chemical abundances across various elemental groups—including light, odd-Z, $\alpha$, Fe-peak, and neutron-capture elements—based on high signal-to-noise spectra of seven giant members. The resulting mean cluster metallicity is determined to be [Fe/H]$=-0.70\pm0.05$, showing no signs of intrinsic metallicity dispersion. Ton~2 displays a standard $\alpha$-enrichment pattern consistent with other high-metallicity Galactic globular clusters, mirroring trends observed in 47~Tucanae and NGC~6380. However, we detect a significant spread in nitrogen abundance ($>0.5$~dex) and a substantial population of nitrogen-enriched stars, indicative of extensive mass transfer from an evolved donor, most likely a former cluster member. Additionally, we identify a $>3\sigma$ excess of sodium-rich stars in Ton~2; these stars also exhibit reduced calcium and magnesium abundances. Regarding iron-peak elements, Ton~2 demonstrates normal ratios of Si, Ca, and Mn relative to Fe, similar to 47~Tucanae, but shows a distinct [Co/Fe] ratio, an observation previously unreported in Galactic globular clusters. Additionally, we find a [Ni/Fe] value of 0.13, suggesting a potential link between Ton~2 and NGC~6380 and 47~Tucanae. While the total [Ni/H] abundance aligns with the typical range for Galactic globular clusters, the elevated [Ni/Fe] suggests a possible overproduction of heavy elements during the cluster's early evolutionary stages. Finally, our analysis of neutron-capture elements reveals a typical [Sr/Fe] ratio, but a [Ba/Fe] level that is more than a factor of two lower than the median for other high-[Fe/H] Galactic globular clusters. We conclude by comparing the chemistry of Ton~2 and NGC~6380, two clusters of comparable ages and dynamical states. Cluster formation models must account for the distinct chemical properties of these systems, particularly the enrichment of odd-Z elements and nitrogen observed in Ton~2

However, these proofs are typically stored in intricate detail, making manual examination time-consuming and impractical for all but the most dedicated studies. In this work, we present the first empirical study of the Isabelle archive that overcomes these challenges. By utilizing a custom-built tool, termed ArchiveMiner, we investigate the growth of the archive from 2004 to 2019 and examine various aspects of proof contributions, including citation patterns, the influence of research areas, and the impact of specific features such as libraries and formalized libraries. Our findings reveal a significant surge in contribution sizes since 2013, a trend attributed to the increased popularity of large-scale projects like the Lean Covertion Tool. Additionally, we analyze how the archive's diversity has shifted over time. These insights are intended to assist researchers in future empirical studies of programming proof systems. We have made the ArchiveMiner tool accessible online.

This model defines a multilayer network as a collection of multiple edge-weighted, potentially directed graphs sharing the same set of nodes, where each graph constitutes a layer and no edges connect nodes across different layers. Similar to standard eigenvector centrality, a node's importance in a specific layer is derived from the weighted sum of its neighbors' importance within that same layer. A key finding is that generalized global $\mathbb{Z}_2$ $\mathcal{N}=4$ $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetries can be circumvented by introducing $\mathbb{C}P^{1}$ bundles over hypermultiplet $\mathbb{C}^{*}$ bases, which generate additional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetries. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the claim regarding $\mathcal{N}=4$ global $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetries found in prior literature [1] applies only to weakly coupled theories; this issue is resolved by incorporating strongly coupled $\mathcal{N}=4$ hypermultiplets in the adjoint representation. We also present a formula to compute generalized global $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetries based on the structure of the $\mathcal{N}=2$ scalar manifold, along with a quantum gravity dual for theories featuring a Hodge number $h^{1,1} X=1$. Additionally, we show that all $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories admit a dual description via $\mathcal{N}=1$ brane constructions [2, 3], which unifies the understanding of their global symmetries. Our results imply that the $\mathcal{N}=1$ field theories described in [4] have no weakly coupled $\mathcal{N}=4$ hypermultiplets and possess no generalized global $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetries. Finally, we provide quantum gravity duals for all $\mathcal{N}=2$ superconformal field theories and those arising from resolving singularities on $\mathbb{C}^{3}$, as well as for all superconformal $\mathcal{N}=1$ field theories. Any $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theory can be viewed as a low-energy limit of $\mathcal{N}=1$ theories, and we provide evidence that their $\mathcal{N}=4$ electric-magnetic $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetries are fully explained by $\mathcal{N}=1$ magnetic symmetries. Our objective is to reduce both the quantity and intricacy of hardware and software elements that users must trust to resist adversarial attacks. We propose a multi-domain hardware architecture featuring statically partitioned, physically isolated trust domains. To facilitate this, we introduce a limited set of simple, formally verified hardware components that allow programs to obtain provably exclusive and simultaneous access to computation and I/O resources temporarily. To oversee this hardware, we developed OctopOS, an operating system built from mutually distrustful subsystems. We implemented a prototype of this system on a CPU-FPGA board, demonstrating that it incurs minimal hardware overhead compared to contemporary System-on-Chip (SoC) designs. For security-critical applications, our machine significantly lowers the required trust compared to standard Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) while maintaining satisfactory performance. For standard applications, performance remains comparable to that of legacy systems. To validate the security guarantees of formallly correct trust boundaries, we executed both synthetic and real-world attacks that attempted to exploit hardware faults (via laser or microwave perturbation), silent hardware errors, and logical vulnerabilities within the TEE. To assess the security of other hardware, we utilized our machine to probe potentially malicious SoCs, successfully detecting hidden malware and temporally coerced side-channel leaks. Finally, to test I/O security, we demonstrated that our machine can successfully desynchronize potentially malicious file systems. Our research indicates that it is feasible to construct secure systems that can either achieve performance comparable to legacy hardware or offer moderate performance for high-security applications, all while minimizing the necessity for user trust. In contrast to conventional security methodologies that aim to contain threats within isolated domains (such as firewalls, sandboxes, and TEEs), our multi-domain machine is designed from the outset to actively defeat adversaries through a variety of formal, hardware-based countermeasures. To accomplish this, we provide a taxonomy of formal counter-strategies that utilize spatial (hardware isolation), temporal (turn-taking), spectral (frequency separation), and physical layer defenses. These counter-strategies are formally verified with the aid of a novel decision procedure for linear arithmetic that operates inside hardware trust domains. To illustrate the practicality of this work, we developed formallly correct applications for secret sharing, secure multi-party computation, and hardware tracing. We propose an attack model featuring an \textit{adaptive} adversary capable of arbitrarily corrupting rewards and transitions at any step within an episode, limited to at most an $\epsilon$-fraction of total learning episodes; this model is strictly more powerful than those in previous studies. Our primary finding establishes that no algorithm can achieve a policy better than $O(\epsilon)$-optimal under these conditions. Subsequently, we demonstrate that the natural policy gradient (NPG) method surprisingly maintains natural robustness when reward corruption is bounded, enabling it to locate an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy. Building on this, we introduce the Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG) algorithm, which tolerates unbounded reward corruption and achieves an $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$-optimal policy. Notably, FPG represents the first approach to provide meaningful learning guarantees when a constant fraction of episodes are corrupted. In addition to theoretical contributions, we validate that a neural network implementation of FPG delivers strong robust learning performance on MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks. Finally, FPG serves as a practical solution that significantly outperforms existing methods in both synthetic adversarial settings and real-world drone learning tasks subjected to attacks. This work advances the field of robust RL by elucidating the inherent difficulties and potential strategies for solving them. Keywords: Robust Reinforcement Learning, Adaptive Attacks, Filtered Policy Gradient.

Robust reinforcement learning examines the challenges of acquiring a effective policy when an adversary corrupts either rewards, transitions, or both. This paper focuses on a novel attack model for MDPs where an adaptive adversary can corrupt both components, subject to a budget measured by the fraction of total learning episodes. Specifically, the adversary may influence a limited fraction $\epsilon$ of episodes, arbitrarily altering rewards and transitions throughout these episodes up to an $\epsilon$-fraction of all time steps. Despite a general impossibility result showing that learning anything beyond an $O(\epsilon)$-optimal policy is impossible under this model, we present two positive results. First, we show that the natural policy gradient (NPG), requiring no modifications, yields an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy given a bound on the reward corruption fraction. Second, we introduce the Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG) algorithm, which achieves an $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$-optimality bound with only an additive $O(1)$ factor in the objective.

This document examines the original box game and various versions of the game introduced in prior discussions. The objective is to demonstrate that, in certain modifications of the box game, players can forecast unknown real numbers with high accuracy despite having no valuable information. The findings presented here are based on the research of E. Feinerman, Y. Katz, A. Levin, and N. Shashar. The game involves two players, Alice and Bob, and three boxes, with a target value $X$. In the original formulation, $X$ is a known non-zero real number. Alice plays first; she selects a box, after which Bob chooses a box for her to open. The box contains a card with a real number $x$. Alice wins if her predicted value for $X$ is closer to $x$ than Bob's prediction is. The central question is whether there exists a pair of strategies for Alice and Bob that gives Alice a winning probability exceeding $1/2$. Feinerman et al. proved that in the original game, Alice and Bob can indeed win with a probability greater than $1/2$. However, we show that this result no longer holds in a version of the game where $X$ is unknown. Furthermore, we demonstrate that even when Alice does not know $X$, she can still win with a probability surpassing $1/2$ if she does not select the box first. We also investigate scenarios where either Bob or Alice lacks knowledge of $X$. While the original game's name does not change if Bob is unaware of $X$, Alice can no longer secure a win probability exceeding $1/2$ without additional assistance. We further find that if Alice does not know $X$, she cannot win with a probability greater than or equal to $1/2$ unless she receives some information about $X$. However, if Alice knows that $X$ is an integer, she can still win with a probability exceeding $1/2$ despite not knowing the specific integer value. Quantum acoustic cavities, capable of sustaining intense field interactions between many-phonon states, can be realized in diverse acoustic platforms. This work presents a comprehensive theory of these systems, specifically examining a crystal slab model that accounts for finite thickness and lateral structure, such as a central defect or dielectric inclusion. This approach offers a fundamental description of both propagating and localized acoustic modes, including their coupling to many-phonon states and a spectrum of nonadiabatic effects. The framework is particularly effective for systems where a narrow frequency band of acoustic waves becomes trapped between the slab's boundaries. It was applied to two scenarios: an amorphous solid (bulk acoustic glass) containing a inclusion, and a bulk crystal with a central interstitial impurity. The theory accurately describes many-phonon spectroscopy, including interference patterns arising from a band of propagating modes, in both localized and glassy bulk acoustic systems. Additionally, it addresses many-phonon decoherence, incorporating the effects of related phonon escape and phonon loss. Ultimately, this formalism provides a foundational understanding for proposing and designing proposals for quantum acoustics devices based on many-phonon phenomena in both glassy and crystal acoustic systems.

Using a nearest-neighbour tight-binding model with horizontal and vertical hopping, we identify two non-equivalent Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone along a high-symmetry trajectory. These cones can be manipulated through various Hamiltonian perturbations that break lattice symmetries; initially, we introduce distinct onsite potentials, which cause the Dirac cones to evolve into semi-Dirac cones and nodal lines along high-symmetry paths. This non-symmorphic herringbone lattice expands our comprehension of band structure dynamics within a Dirac scenario and reveals the potential for engineering exotic states of matter, such as nodal lines and Dirac cones, via Hamiltonian parameter tuning. Because these infinite-dimensional problems frequently lack known analytical solutions, numerical methods are required to find approximate answers. This paper introduces a unified notation to describe key techniques within the transcription phase of simultaneous direct methods (specifically the discretize-then-optimize approach) for solving continuous-time dynamic optimization problems. The discussion highlights collocation, integrated residual, and Runge-Kutta schemes. These methods are applied to a simulation case study addressing a question from the COVID-19 pandemic: can a single ventilator treat multiple patients when supplies are scarce? The findings indicate that, in principle, individual patient parameters can be estimated with sufficient accuracy using a limited number of flow rate measurements, without disconnecting patients or requiring additional sensors. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that two patients can receive their required tidal volumes by adjusting the air flow resistance for each and controlling ventilator pressure. The problem formulation and results were validated by a medical expert. Finally, the paper emphasizes that these findings rely on the accuracy of the numerical solution to the transcription of the continuous-time optimization problem. Correctness checks are proposed to ensure that discrete problems capture the essential features of their continuous counterparts, noting that these checks are crucial when the discretize-then-optimize approach is used, particularly when high-order integrators are employed at low discretization densities. This study investigates whether a streamlined clinical workflow relying solely on CT imaging can enable high-quality automatic segmentation of esophageal tumors. To address this, we introduce a fully automatic, end-to-end segmentation method utilizing Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Furthermore, dilated convolutional layers are implemented to expand the network's receptive field while optimizing GPU memory usage. We assembled a dataset comprising 165 cases from over 100,00 axial slices, split into training and testing sets. The model was trained on this data and subsequently evaluated on the test cases. Quantitative results demonstrate that the DDAUnet achieved a Hausdorff Distance of 25.17mm and a Dice coefficient of 89.6% on the testing set. bons are frequently found in complex reservoirs, making real-time optimized well placement (geosteering) essential for effective production and cost reduction. This process typically relies on updated formation evaluations derived from real-time well-log interpretation. Therefore, a key challenge is extracting K–V (kernel – vector) representations of acoustic logging measurements for subsequent classification and regression to estimate critical properties like packer position, casing collars, and water saturation. This work introduces a regression-based estimator for sandstone formations that predicts ultrasonic transmission and reflection coefficients. These predictions are generated by learning a representation of the mixture of acoustic paths through various interface geometries, specifically focusing on four to five dominant triangular regions (bases) defined by their geometry, the rock's flatness, and adjacent material properties. Unlike previous approaches that modeled each base independently, our method utilizes a softmax-linked neural network to learn a global representation of the entire base-of-the-well distribution of acoustical paths. This learning occurs off-line through an iterative update scheme that connects observed logarithmic co-variances of acoustic coefficients to an uncertainty measure, thereby improving efficiency and reducing overfitting. The proposed solution was validated using over 10,000 logs from a single well in the North Sea, demonstrating prediction errors of less than 0.03 for transmission coefficients and 0.5% for water saturation. Furthermore, the method is general enough to handle multiple formations and can be tailored to handle online well-specific adjustments. In an era of remote and real-time well operations, this solution is general enough to be deployed as a mobile application for geosteering support. We conclude by proposing solutions for vertically and laterally constrained next-generation wells. Overall, our contributions advance real-time estimated well evaluation for complex reservoirs, offering an integrated solution for geosteering that is applicable to drilling operations worldwide.

Our objective is to calculate a reliable estimate of formation density using an ensemble of deep learning algorithms. Specifically, we train multiple neural network-based estimators, each specializing in distinct frequency bands and depth intervals to handle the heterogeneous nature of reservoir data. To produce a robust density prediction, we employ an ensemble strategy that aggregates the outputs of these diverse estimators. The general architecture of this ensemble is determined by a learning-to-learning approach, which optimizes the structure based on the spatial distribution of the training data. Our results show that this proposed method significantly outperforms individual specialized estimators and existing baseline solutions across various onshore and offshore oil and gas wells.

Nested NER, a specific subset of NER, involves named entities that are contained within one another. However, many prior studies on nested NER utilize linear structures to model entities that inherently possess a hierarchical organization. To resolve this discrepancy, this work treats all nested entities within a sentence as a unified structure and introduces a structure-aware attention mechanism to facilitate effective entity extraction. Additionally, we propose two new structure-based classification approaches to resolve extraction conflicts: a parallel structure classification method for entities with the same type, and a hierarchical structure classification method for entities with different types. Experiments conducted on two public datasets, SNER and CKS, demonstrate that our proposed methods surpass current state-of-the-art techniques. Specifically, the F1 score for nested entity recognition in our approach reaches 81.18%, exceeding the highest score of 79.88% achieved by existing methods. Furthermore, we assessed the performance of previous baseline methods alongside our baseline on a low-resource domain-specific dataset to evaluate the model's adaptability to new domains. These findings indicate that our model not only performs superiorly within specialized domains but also generalizes effectively to new domains with minimal additional training. The code for this research is accessible at https://github.com/ndphuongnguyen/Structure-Aware-NER. We hope our model will contribute to future efforts in low-resource nested NER and related low-resource natural language processing tasks.

Recent years have seen a surge in research on robust deep learning, with a specific focus on deep few-shot learning (FSL), which enables the rapid acquisition of new knowledge using only a small dataset. This field is vital for rapidly evolving domains where collecting extensive, high-quality training data is difficult, costly, or time-consuming. For instance, in disease diagnosis, new conditions frequently emerge, necessitating classification systems trained on large, condition-specific datasets. While existing literature offers various strategies to enhance FSL accuracy, these approaches often rely on complex modules or pre-trained networks, which are difficult to adapt to data with scarce labels. This paper presents a novel and simple framework for FSL designed to deliver accurate results with few labels while avoiding the need for extensive fine-tuning or heavy pre-training. Our method, which leverages prototype-basedFSL for maximum flexibility and minimum parameter count, employs three key components: (1) an uncertainty-aware prototype generation module to produce reliable prototypes under overfitting pressure, (2) a max-entropy loss function to maximize prediction entropy on support data via max-pooling over feature embeddings, and (3) an adaptive sample weight generation module to create sample-wise weights for balanced prototype calculation. Experiments across \textit{mini}ImageNet, \textit{tiered}ImageNet, and cross-domain settings demonstrate our method's superiority over both recent and traditional baselines. Since our approach requires only a lightweight fully-connected layer for prototype adaptation, it is highly practical for immediate application in FSL without the constraints of complex optimization or reliance on pre-trained weights.

The paper titled "Rigid-Body Swarms Exhibiting Flexible Shapes Through Reciprocal Thrusts" analyzes the motion capabilities of a group of free-flying, nonholonomic vehicles capable of individual orientation control. This system, formulated as proportional thrust swarms, enables vectors summing to zero, allowing the swarm to execute zero net translation while performing in-place rotations, expansions, contractions, and various periodic behaviors. Although prior work has simulated these swarm dynamics, they have not yet been rigorously examined using methods from classical mechanics. This work rigorously investigates the dynamic and kinematic properties of proportional thrust swarms, including their ability to generate time-varying moments, angular accelerations, and angular velocities. By employing spherical harmonics, we characterize the velocity field produced by the swarm and determine the conditions under which leading-order approximations yield circular motions, elliptical orbits, and other stable periodic trajectories for individual vehicles. Additionally, we utilize an optimization-based approach to demonstrate that proportional thrust swarms can achieve the same periodic orbits targeted by recent studies on visual ring and diamond formations. Although the specific control laws differ, the periodic orbits are mathematically identical, proving that proportional thrust swarms can match the performance of more sophisticated nonlinear control protocols. Deep detectors leverage scene context in distinct ways. This study categorizes object detectors into three groups based on their context utilization: those with no context (RCNN via input cropping), those with partial context (two-stage methods via featuremap cropping), and those with full context (single-stage methods without cropping). We systematically assess the impact of context across these detector categories by constructing a fully controlled dataset with varying contextual conditions and analyzing context usage in deep detectors. Furthermore, we evaluate the effects of progressively removing background and foreground elements on the MS COCO dataset. Our findings indicate that both single-stage and two-stage detectors inherently utilize context through their extensive receptive fields, suggesting that the optimal detector choice often depends on the specific application context. Finally, we examine context usage within current trending architectures, such as those utilizing SwinTR and C2f modules. We hope this analysis of context usage across receptive fields, model designs, and architectures promotes its broader adoption in future computer vision research.

### 1 Introduction

The Yahoo! Knowledge Graph is a structured dataset comprising entities extracted from various online knowledge bases, with Wikipedia serving as its primary source. These entities and their interconnections are ideally recommended to users based on context, such as query intent or profile information. The End-to-End Entity Recommendation framework described in this study generates context-aware proposals by analyzing entity contents and graph topologies through a multi-view approach combined with a rank-based integration strategy. This work functions as a generic framework applicable to diverse offline and online evaluation settings. Specifically, this paper focuses on a simple yet effective embedding method for producing high-quality entity recommendations within a Wikipedia environment. This method, termed "ReWIE" (Recommendation in Wiki via Embedding Embedentities and Neighboring Entities), was developed to deliver contextualized suggestions by leveraging the topological features of multi-scale layered Wikipedia graphs. ReWIE produces contextualized entity representations by integrating features derived from topologically similar entities and those frequently linked across different scales, using a linear learning-to-rank classifier to propose related entities. These proposals are validated through rigorous offline and interactive online evaluations. Our findings indicate that ReWIE significantly outperforms existing baselines. While re-ranking techniques yield marginal improvements, they increase latency, making reWIE more than ten times faster than the current Yahoo! Knowledge Graph retrieval system. Consequently, ReWIE has been deployed as the default entity recommendation engine for the site navigation component of both Yahoo! and Bing.

This study investigates the optimal acceptance strategies for potentially incompatible kidneys tailored to individual patients with end-stage kidney disease. To model the impact of incompatibility, we introduce a Markov Decision Process (MDP) framework that treats compatibility as an explicit state variable. Although this results in a higher-dimensional model that complicates analysis, we derive structural properties—specifically control limit-type optimal policies—that are straightforward to calculate and apply. Numerical simulations demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves across varying mismatch levels and underscore the necessity of integrating incompatibility status directly into acceptance decisions, particularly when desensitization therapy is available. As a byproduct, we provide a detailed characterization of the incompatibility cost, defined as the reduction in survival benefits for undialyzed patients due to incompatibility; this metric is essential for valuing kidneys in economic models of transplantation. The findings from this and related papers will inform a forthcoming randomized controlled trial. This work advances the body of literature on organ exchange networks, osteopath allocation, and donation from living relatives. This overview introduces and reviews this extensive category, encompassing elliptical copulas, skew $t$ copulas, factor copulas, time series copulas, and regression copulas. It details the standard auxiliary representation that underpins these models, explaining how this framework ensures scalability and tractability for statistical analysis. Key challenges are examined, including parameter identification, the use of extended likelihoods for discrete or mixed data, maintaining parsimony in high dimensions, and simulation procedures. The text also outlines Bayesian techniques for estimating parameters and generating predictions from implicit copula models. Significant focus is placed on implicit copula processes derived from time series and regression models, which currently represent a leading area of research. Finally, two econometric case studies—one involving macroeconomic time series and the other addressing financial asset pricing—demonstrate the benefits of utilizing implicit copula models. These discussions provide references to broader literature on specific topics and offer links to related review papers. Throughout the manuscript, equations are validated using the R statistical package, specifically packages like `mcop` and `bayesimplicitcopula`.

Bayesian inference for implicit copula processes represents a promising area of modern statistical research. This review paper outlines the advantages of this approach for time series analysis and provides a review of recent advancements, highlighting both theoretical findings and practical applications. While many implicit copula processes are built upon linear factor models or univariate time series models, recent developments have created models that capture non-linear dependencies and apply to multivariate time series. Although these models offer significant potential, they remain in an early stage, with many challenges remaining regarding their application to real-world data. The paper illustrates the practical difficulties of fitting implicit copula processes using two case studies based on multivariate time series and count data. These examples demonstrate the need for further research into computational methods for estimating parameters, generating simulations, and performing predictions with implicit copula processes. Additionally, the work addresses issues surrounding model specification, such as selection, identification, and parsimony. Throughout the discussion, the benefits of the implicit copula framework are emphasized, particularly regarding interpretability and computational efficiency when handling multivariate time series. The appendix lists references related to implicit copula processes and their applications in time series analysis. Throughout the document, R code is provided to illustrate the examples and verify the results.

We all possess distinct biological and behavioral characteristics that set us apart, yet we frequently overlook these differences when perceiving one another. Our primary goal is to investigate the factors driving successful collaborations between biological entities, such as cells, and humans, for instance, in the administration of cancer treatments. To achieve this, we propose a systematic framework for examining human-bio interactions, which serves to structure and clarify existing literature on the subject. Subsequently, we apply this framework to explore various critical topics within the field, including the origins of off-target effects in pharmacology, the mechanisms by which cells develop tolerance to biological agents, and how syntonic and disharmonious pheromones influence rat behavioral patterns. Although diverse in nature, these phenomena can be categorized and structured using the proposed human-bio interaction types. Ultimately, we summarize key open questions and potential future research directions in this domain.

We formulate optimization problems aimed at maximizing both fair-throughput and sum-throughput. Leveraging a fixed-point based alternating algorithm, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput solutions for both SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM configurations. Numerical results demonstrate that our proposed OFDM strategies achieve a fair-throughput almost identical to the optimal wideband widebeam solution presented in [1]. Additionally, the OFDM solutions prove superior in terms of spectrum efficiency and computational complexity. It is important to note that the specific optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput outcomes vary depending on the channel model employed, as discussed in [2]. These system designs are intended to operate in scenarios where the receiver possesses only coarse channel state information (CSI). Our findings indicate that the performance gain in fair-throughput between the optimal widebeam method from [1] and the current OFDM designs is almost negligible when the number of receive antennas is 1 or when channel estimation inaccuracy is high. However, the gain in sum-throughput is always positive and can be substantially large, provided that the channel estimation inaccuracy is not extremely minimal. Furthermore, we establish that the proposed fair-throughput solutions yield almost the same performance in terms of both metrics, to be precise. These systems find application in environments with moderate channel fluctuations, offering two key advantages: 1) maximizing throughput, and 2) delivering optimal computational complexity, as optimal widebeam solutions are computationally prohibitive under rapid channel fluctuation conditions where channel estimation is uncertain. Additionally, the OFDM solutions significantly simplify receiver design by eliminating the need for complex and costly optimal waveforming techniques. The paper also clarifies that the proposed OFDM solutions are not applicable in settings with perfect channel estimation, as such scenarios necessitate different approaches. In those cases, all users can be treated as a single aggregate link, enabling an optimal widebeam solution to deliver higher throughput. This study introduces an extended two-fluid level-set method for solving the Navier--Stokes equations involving a moving contact line. By employing this framework, we simulate a liquid droplet sliding on a solid surface with variable contact angles. The contact angle is modified smoothly within a thin region near the three-phase contact line by adjusting the boundary condition on the grid cells intersected by the contact line. We examine the contact line's movement under surface tension alone and varying contact angles. Furthermore, we simulate a droplet sliding on a rough surface where the contact line is pinned, demonstrating that the method can effectively handle the jump stress caused by surface roughness.

These controlled operations generate derivational ambiguities that the original Lambek Calculus and its pregroup variant fail to capture. Although proposals exist for interpreting extended Lambek Calculus compositionally within the compact closed category of FVect and linear maps, these approaches treat syntax-semantics mappings as ignoring the control modalities, thereby limiting their influence to syntax alone. Our objective is to elevate these modalities to first-class status within the vectorial interpretation. Leveraging directional density matrix semantics, we expand the type system's interpretation by incorporating an additional spin density matrix space. Consequently, proof interpretations tensor ambiguous derivations with orthogonal spin states. This methodology offers a mechanism for concurrently representing multiple interpretations of ambiguous sentences and establishes a framework for integrating them at the vectorial level. We illustrate this approach using the standard grammatical analysis of "Big Ben rang eleven," demonstrating how it accommodates both traditional and probabilistic semantics for ambiguous inputs. In summary, we present a technique for managing derivational ambiguity within the type interpretation of formal grammars. This works particularly well when incorporating probabilistic weights, effectively handling lexical and derivational ambiguity as a weighted sum of vectors in the feature space. To our knowledge, our work is the first to explicitly address derivational ambiguity in the type interpretation of formal grammars. Furthermore, we integrate probabilistic formulations to manage both lexical and derivational ambiguity, treating them as a combined weighted sum of vectors within feature space. We hope these insights will enhance the handling of formal grammars in downstream natural language processing applications. We begin by outlining the background and motivations for our research. Subsequently, we define the categorical semantics of the pregroup and lambda calculi, extending them to incorporate binary relational interpretation and probability. Finally, we demonstrate how this framework resolves ambiguities in the classic "Big Ben" example. Our proposed extension to the categorical semantics of pregrams and lambda calculi enables the concurrent handling of lexical and derivational form ambiguities. Specifically, we illustrate how interpretations of these ambiguities combine as a weighted sum of vectors, effectively managing form ambiguity. Our work represents an initial step toward creating NLP data structures that can form features within the conventional vectorial lambda calculus interpretation, which underpins programs like Universal Representation for NLP and BERT. This integration would allow NLP systems to utilize syntactic information for handling out-of-vocabulary words and morphological morphology, even when processing languages for which no direct neural program exists. Future work will expand upon these ideas. We

Nevertheless, in the fundamental context of multiplayer general-sum games, current algorithms necessitate an exponential number of samples relative to the player count to learn rationalizable equilibria under bandit feedback. This paper introduces the first family of efficient algorithms capable of learning rationalizable Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) with sample complexities that are polynomial in every problem parameter, including the number of players. To accomplish this, we also propose a new, efficient method for identifying a single rationalizable action profile (which need not be an equilibrium), significantly improving upon the sample complexity achieved by Wu et al. (2021). Our approach integrates several innovative techniques to ensure both rationalizability and no (swap-)regret, such as a correlated exploration scheme and adaptive learning rates, which may hold independent value. We further validate our findings with a sample complexity lower bound that demonstrates the tightness of our guarantees. At the core of our analysis lies a meticulous comparison between the correlated and pure regret frameworks, enabling a careful and rigorous evaluation of the algorithms' performance. In summary, this work establishes a foundational framework for the design and analysis of multiagent learning algorithms aimed at achieving rationalizable behavior.

Recently, Wu et al. (2021) demonstrated an exponential sample complexity gap between pure and correlated regret in the task of learning a rationalizable equilibrium. This work presents a more substantial gap of $d^3$ between these two settings when the goal is to learn a single rationalizable action, as defined by Hart and Nair (2020). Our contributions encompass both novel algorithms and innovative analytical methods. Our findings are particularly relevant to the open challenge of reducing the $d$ dependency in $O(d^2)$ complexity results by Alon et al. (2022) and Hong et al. (2022) for rationalizable CCE. The network structure follows an Erdős–Rényi random graph, but susceptible individuals adjacent to infectious nodes may sever or rewire these links during the epidemic. We derive large-population limits that establish convergence for the initial branching process phase and, under the assumption of a major outbreak, for the subsequent epidemic phase, which approaches a deterministic model equivalent to a specific pair approximation. Additionally, we obtain law of large numbers results for the final size of a major outbreak. Two key findings emerge across various parameter configurations: (i) the limiting proportion of infected individuals can exhibit a discontinuity at the critical infection rate $\lambda_c$, resulting in an abrupt jump from zero to a positive value, and (ii) when rewiring is restricted to uninfected individuals, this discontinuity causes the final infected fraction to leap from $0$ to $1$ as $\lambda$ crosses $\lambda_c$. These observations indicate that the critical behavior of the model can vary significantly depending on parameters, with discontinuities in the infected fraction driving these differences. This contrasts with models lacking rewiring or where rewiring involves only infected individuals, scenarios where the infected fraction changes continuously and the effective reproduction number remains valid at criticality. Our proofs rely on establishing a link between the epidemic process and the Hopf–Langevin equation for a certain random matrix process. Digital objective statements align with our research profile. The findings presented here extend those of [K. Garas and G. R. Grimmett, Phys. Rev. E {\bf 92}, 042804 (2015)]. Our analysis examines a stochastic SIR epidemic model on a social network where the probability of an edge connecting an infectious node to a susceptible one can be updated based on the current edge distribution. For a large network, we demonstrate that given a minor outbreak, the initial phase converges to a Galton-Watson process, while the final infected fraction does so for the major outbreak phase. A key contribution of this paper is providing insights into the critical point and the often-discontinuous jump in the final infected fraction. These results are achieved by relating the stochastic system to a deterministic limit and utilizing large deviation theory. Subsequently, assuming the potential vector field is orthogonal to the Reeb vector field, we prove that on a non-Kenmotsu almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifold where the Reeb vector field is an eigenvector of the Ricci operator, the Cotton soliton is steady and the manifold is locally isometric to $\mathbb{H}^2(-4) \times \mathbb{R}$. Furthermore, if the Ricci operator is a general eigenvector field, the Cotton soliton remains steady, but the condition of the manifold being locally isometric to $\mathbb{H}^2(-4) \times \mathbb{R}$ cannot be established. Finally, we explore the scenario where the potential vector field has a non-constant inner product with the Reeb vector field; in this case, the Cotton soliton is steady, and the manifold is locally isometric to $\mathbb{R}^3$ or $S^2 \times \mathbb{R}$. The paper also includes several other interesting findings regarding Cotton solitons on almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. We also address the converse problem, showing that a non-Kenmotsu almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifold admitting a Cotton soliton with a non-null Killing vector field is locally isometric to $\mathbb{R}^3$ or $S^2 \times \mathbb{R}$. Additionally, if the Ricci operator is an eigenvector field and the scalar curvature $h$ is non-zero, the manifold is locally isometric to $\mathbb{R}^3$. Similar results are derived for gradient Cotton solitons. The paper concludes with a section of remarks and questions. Several findings are supported by the following references: [1] C. O. Arroyo, C. Furthermore, because processes are measured across different scales, the PDF candidate requires DGLAP evolution, either calculated dynamically or precomputed into grids. While classical experience replay enables agents to retain knowledge by reusing past observations, its uniform sampling strategy treats all data points equally, neglecting their varying significance. To address this, we introduce a general Variance Reduction-based Experience Replay (VRER) framework that selectively prioritizes the most relevant samples to refine policy gradient estimates. This adaptive mechanism assigns greater weight to historical data more likely to originate from the current target distribution. Both theoretical analysis and empirical results demonstrate that VRER accelerates the convergence to an optimal policy and boosts the performance of leading policy optimization methods. Yet, even for the extensively researched optimally-doped (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$, significant controversies persist regarding these features. We address these discrepancies by performing high-resolution angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) on the material using both Helium lamps and laser sources. Our findings reveal that the "flat band" near the Brillouin zone center in the superconducting state results from a combination of superconductivity-induced band back-bending and the folding of a band from the zone corner to the center. We provide direct evidence of this band folding in both the normal and superconducting states. By clarifying the origin of the flat band, we can accurately assign the three hole-like bands around the zone center and determine their superconducting gaps. Around the zone corner, we simultaneously observe a tiny electron-like band and an M-shaped band in both states. The derived gap size for these corner bands ($\sim$5.5 meV) is markedly smaller than those reported in previous ARPES studies. These results define a novel superconducting gap structure for optimally-doped (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ and offer essential insights for future theoretical investigations into its superconductivity. Furthermore, our findings suggest that certain features in the Fe-4s core level binding energy reported in prior ARPES literature can be attributed to band folding. Finally, we show that the band folding effect can be modeled as a superposition of two square lattices.

Our analysis of the normal-state structure around the zone center reveals a complex band pattern consistent with superposition band calculations based on the actual crystal structure. The analysis utilizes a dataset of proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 8 TeV, yielding an integrated luminosity of 19.7 $\mathrm{fb^{-1}}$. A high-purity selection of $t$-channel single top quark events featuring an isolated muon is employed, with signal and background contributions determined through a data-driven fit. Following corrections for detector effects, a differential cross section is measured for an angular variable sensitive to polarization. Utilizing this differential distribution, a top quark spin asymmetry of $0.26 \pm 0.03 \texm{(stat)} \pm 0.10 \texm{(syst)}$ is extracted. This result aligns with the Standard Model prediction of 0.44, corresponding to a p-value of 4.6%. Furthermore, the analysis constrains a new physics parameter $\alpha$ in sequential gauge invariant effective field theory, with a 95% confidence level limit of $|\alpha|<0.14 \texm{(syst)}$. The limit incorporating statistical uncertainty is slightly tighter at $|\alpha|<0.11 \texm{(stat+syst)}$. Additionally, the limit on the fraction of single top quark production via the s-channel, $f_{\mathrm{s}}$, is improved to $f_{\mathrm{s}}<0.048 \texm{(syst)}$. This represents a significant enhancement over the preceding world record of $f_{\mathrm{s}}<0.17 \texm{(syst)}$. Finally, the study confirms that the matrix element method for $t$-channel single top quark production is robust against perturbative uncertainties arising from higher-order QCD corrections. The findings also establish a path for leveraging LHC data for precision measurements of polarization in single top quark production at the energy scale of the electroweak phase transition. Index terms: single top quark, spin asymmetry, top quark production, electroweak phase transition.

Spin-lattice relaxation measurements conducted at 6.55 T identified two components of equal amplitude: one displaying metallic behavior with a $T$-linear $1/T_{1}$, and another exhibiting a more intricate temperature dependence. The metallic nature of the slow-relaxing component remains largely insensitive to changes in LaNiO$_3$ thickness, whereas the fast component shows significant sensitivity, particularly in the thinnest, most magnetic samples where it displays an inverse temperature dependence (increasing as $T$ decreases). The underlying causes of this bipartite relaxation are discussed. This result confirms the presence of strongly correlated electrons within a metal and highlights the importance of electronic inhomogeneity, a finding that aligns with recent theoretical predictions. Introduced in 1973, $\beta$-detected NMR offers exceptional chemical sensitivity to the electronic environment, making it a potent tool for probing correlated electron systems. Recent implementations have probed charge ordering in manganites and various aspects of the strange metal state in heavy-fermion and layered transition metal compounds. However, to date, $\beta$-detected NMR has not been utilized to examine correlated oxide superlattices. Achieving high-resolution NMR in these structures required a sensitive detector, which was only possible with the high-efficiency neutron detector available at the Spallation Neutron Source.

We introduce the MultiTalk Dataset, a collection exceeding 320,000 written dialogue sentences that achieves a balance between multiple plausible continuations and coherent meaning. We propose the use of dialogue summarization as a method for training and evaluating models in conversational contexts governed by multiple correct responses. Consequently, we conduct dialogue summarization tasks on the MultiTalk Dataset, summarizing texts with varying numbers of preceding turns. Our experiments assess both single-step and multi-step summarization performances, examining summaries generated both with and without assistance from a reference summary. Our contributions include introducing a conversational dataset suitable for multi-step dialogue summarization, presenting models for this task, and performing comprehensive evaluations using automatic metrics (BLEU, ROC-STALM, and ROC-ALM) and human evaluation. Finally, we establish baselines for single-turn and multi-turn dialogue summarization, achieving an BLEU score of 0.2939 and a human score of 2.33/5 on the test set. Additionally, we demonstrate that models performing single-turn summarization are significantly more likely to generate human-preferred outputs than those trained exclusively on first-turn summaries. Finally, we show that models trained on summaries of the first five turns of a conversation are 1.72 times more likely to continue a dialogue correctly compared to those trained only on first-turn summaries. Our findings indicate that multi-turn dialogue summarization effectively handles conversations with multiple correct continuations. Code is available at https://github.com/AniruddhaChakraborty103/Dialogue_Summariization. Additionally, our code has been selected as a featured publication on GitHub. These results highlight the accessibility and utility of open-source projects within the artificial intelligence community. Our work emphasizes the importance of exploring conversational AI through multi-turn summarization. It is a testament to the accessibility and utility of open-source initiatives in artificial intelligence. Furthermore, our findings underscore the necessity of investigating conversational agents capable of handling multiple correct continuations. This research serves as a foundation for developing more natural and engaging dialog systems. Future studies should build upon this work to create agents that maintain coherence across extended interactions. It would also be valuable to explore these concepts in multilingual settings or with enhanced evaluation metrics. Such endeavors will advance our understanding of conversational intelligence. Unlike many existing studies, we explicitly consider the impact of correlated Rayleigh fading and the coupling between the amplitude and phase shifts of each IRS element's reflection coefficient, factors often overlooked despite their practical relevance. Leveraging random matrix theory, we derive a closed-form probability density function (PDF) for the cascaded channel, from which the EC is calculated based solely on large-scale statistics and phase shifts. We further optimize the EC with respect to phase shifts using a low-overhead approach, updating the parameters only every few coherence intervals rather than relying on computationally intensive frequent optimizations based on instantaneous channel data. Monte-Carlo simulations confirm our analytical findings and reveal the critical interactions among key parameters and their influence on the system's EC. Our results demonstrate that, in large-scale deployments, the derived closed-form expressions remain highly accurate. Additionally, the proposed closed-form expressions for EC and the suggested low-overhead optimization method significantly reduce signaling overhead. In contrast, when the number of transmitters and receivers is small, the closed-form expressions may overestimate the EC, a scenario that is addressed via numerical optimization. Finally, simulations explore EC maximization in deployments consisting of multiple IRSs. # Introduction

This section provides an overview of $\tau$-tilting theory, outlining the representation theoretic problems it solves and how it extends the framework of classical tilting theory.

## Representation Theory and Tilting

Representation theory seeks to apply the efficient methods of abstract algebra—such as composition series, homological invariants, and duality—to the rich structures of groups, rings, and modules by studying their associated representations.

Until relatively recently, the field was largely divided into two distinct areas. One branch, often linked to specific mathematical structures like groups or geometric objects, utilized tools from linear algebra, combinatorics, and topology. The other, deeply rooted in category theory and homological algebra, relied on concepts such as derived categories, Ext-groups, and triangulated categories.

While this specialization allowed for significant progress, it also created a barrier to unifying the field. To overcome this, researchers in representation theory now actively seek to merge these diverse representation categories with the powerful techniques of homological algebra and category theory.

A pivotal development in this unification effort is $\tau$-tilting theory. It generalizes classical tilting theory to any finite length category—specifically, any category equivalent to the module category of a finite quiver with relations—thereby providing access to desirable properties like duality and composition series within $\tau$-tilting theory itself.

To understand $\tau$-tilting theory, one must first grasp the representation theory of quivers, a field pioneered by Samuel P. Eisenbud in the late 1950s.

Multi-agent systems are capable of addressing tasks unattainable by individual agents, yet their success often hinges on their capacity to overcome challenges of varying complexities. We investigate how agents with limited computation and communication ranges can coordinate to execute two such tasks. Our primary finding indicates that an agent restricted to using a linear model of other agents' behaviors (and communication) typically outperforms an agent utilizing a constant or null strategy. Additionally, we demonstrate that an agent employing a linear behavior model can identify which tasks are feasible to complete. These results were verified through both simulations and a hardware experiment featuring multiple Raspberry Pi agents on an outdoor platform. This paper is a revised and expanded version of the preliminary work reported in \cite{farhadi21b}.

approach enabling multiple parties to collaboratively train robust machine learning models without exchanging their sensitive data. Based on collaboration structures, FL is categorized into Horizontal Federated Learning (HFL) and Vertical Federated Learning (VFL). In HFL, entities share identical feature spaces and data samples, whereas in VFL, they share common sample identifiers and collaborate on features. VFL offers a wider application scope and is particularly well-suited for joint model training among large enterprises.

This paper concentrates on VFL, examining potential privacy vulnerabilities within real-world frameworks. We developed and executed two practical privacy attacks: a reverse multiplication attack targeting the logistic regression VFL protocol and a reverse sum attack targeting the XGBoost VFL protocol. Our empirical analysis demonstrates that these attacks are (1) effective, allowing adversaries to extract private training data even when intermediate outputs are encrypted; (2) evasive, as they adhere strictly to protocol specifications and do not degrade the target model's accuracy; and (3) low-effort, requiring minimal prior knowledge of the target participant's data distribution. Furthermore, we show that the information leaked is as potent as the original training data for training alternative classifiers. Finally, we discuss potential countermeasures and their associated challenges, aiming to inspire future research directions. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/MyWayLife/Reversing_VFL.

In summary, we introduce a general methodology for assessing the privacy risks of VFL. This work underscores the significance of privacy within VFL protocols and provides a working example of how such protocols may be compromised. These findings will help raise awareness of privacy concerns in VFL and inform the design of systems that strengthen protocol robustness against future threats.

To overcome this, Random Fourier Features (RFF) were introduced to approximate kernel functions using randomized Fourier features, enabling scalability. Despite its popularity, RFF has notable limitations: because it samples features from a distribution independent of the training data, it demands a large number of feature dimensions to match the performance of kernelized classifiers, a requirement that scales with dataset size. This paper introduces Pseudo Random Fourier Features (PRFF), a data-dependent kernel approximation technique designed to minimize feature dimensions and enhance predictive performance. The method is evaluated on classification and regression tasks, with comparisons made against RFF, orthogonal random features, and the Nyström approach. Practical implementations of PRFF are available on GitHub at https://github.com/Ahmed-6666/PRFF. Grounded in network percolation theory, we examine the "avalanche" effect triggered by the removal of a single node from the giant component—a phenomenon where one removal causes a cascade of disconnections that significantly contributes to network fragmentation and immunization beyond the loss of that single node. We specifically analyze the avalanche size, defined as the count of nodes disconnected from the giant component due to one removal. Furthermore, regarding random attacks on Cayley tree networks, we derive the general formula for avalanche size and its distribution using percolation theory, along with calculating the "avalanche threshold" ($\phi_a$) and its variance. Our findings reveal that for random attacks on Cayley tree networks, the avalanche threshold is given by $\phi_a=1-1/k$, where $k$ represents the branching factor. Additionally, the avalanche size distribution follows a power law, indicating that while most attacks result in small avalanches, there is a non-zero probability of large-scale events that could cause major disruptions. Consequently, attack strategies should not solely focus on achieving power law avalanche distributions, as this does not necessarily guarantee the network's complete disconnection or survival. The derived formulas offer insights into the resilience of Cayley tree networks, the architecture of the internet, and the propagation of misinformation and epidemics. The work is concluded by proposing potential directions for future research. Until then, the study advocates adopting a holistic perspective that integrates both micro-level processes and macro-level phenomena in attack analysis. Finally, we provide the necessary equations supporting our claims and the source code for all simulations presented. Throughout the paper, we have also included citations linking to the provided equations and source code. Various citations are offered to help readers navigate the material and locate the corresponding source code. Additionally, we present general citations applicable to the entire paper. Throughout our analysis, we have utilized sources to validate our statements, and we have organized the paper into sections for clarity. We have structured the manuscript into different parts to ensure a logical flow. To verify the accuracy of our results, we encourage the community to examine our provided source code. We present two distinct methods for calculating the $g$-function of the compactification of the universal family of stable rank 2 torsion free sheaves, $X_S(r,c^2,\chi)$, on the universal surface $S$ within a fixed moduli chart. The first method relies on the reflection equality for $g$-functions established in \cite{CKL2}, while the second provides a direct computation via Riemann--Roch calculations and $\chi$ genus additivity. For small values of $r$, both approaches yield identical results, implying that $X_S(r,c^2,\chi)$ is $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano if and only if it is toric. However, when $r=5$ and $(r,c^2,\chi)=(5,0,6)$, the computation reveals a $\delta$ invariant of $\frac{7}{6}$, indicating the variety is not toric.

Specifically, for the first two cases, we establish generating functions representing the total number of deepest nodes and compute their averages. We define a marked ordered tree as a directed tree with a distinguished descendant of the root; the depth of the tree corresponds to the shortest path length from this distinguished node to an endnode. Let $t_n$ represent the set of marked ordered trees with $n$ endnodes. We demonstrate that the average depth of a tree selected uniformly at random from $t_n$ approaches $2$ as $n$ tends to infinity. This extends the classical finding by Sch\"afer and Shattuck regarding marked binary trees, where the average mark count also approaches $2$. Our proof utilizes the depth generating function, a method previously employed by Gouyou-Beauchamps to characterize the distribution of depths in marked binary trees.

While the structure of marked ordered trees is comprehensive, the specific context in which average depth arises and its relationship to other properties in this domain require further clarification. This paper introduces a low-complexity deep learning approach designed for on-device speech enhancement in low-resource, low-latency environments. The system employs a bidirectional autoencoder structure where the decoder utilizes an efficient attention mechanism. Attention helps mitigate errors caused by noisy training data, a benefit particularly valuable outside large-scale datasets. These rooms maintain internal pressure lower than the surrounding environment to ensure pathogen containment. Currently, Building Management Systems (BMSs) rely on differential pressure (DP) sensors to monitor NPR pressure; however, these sensors are prone to drifting and failing over time. This study investigated the functionality and safety of a NPR located in an infectious-control hospital in South Korea, focusing on its DP sensor performance. Our results revealed that while the DP sensor for negative pressure was generally functional, it exhibited a significant failure rate, potentially risking pathogen leakage. Negative Pressure Rooms (NPRs) are essential for preventing pathogen leakage in infection-control hospitals. Although differential pressure (DP) sensors are used to maintain NPR safety, they frequently malfunction and require maintenance. This study monitored a NPR in Seoul, South Korea, for 24 hours, focusing on the functionality and safety of its DP sensors. Although this phenomenon is often blamed on forecasting inaccuracies or operational breakdowns, we argue it stems from risk-averse scheduling strategies. By applying a stochastic self-scheduling model to real-world data from the Australian National Electricity Market, we show that risk-averse storage units adopt a short-sighted operational approach. Specifically, they focus primarily on near-term price arbitrage, targeting only a limited number of extreme price peaks and valleys, which leaves them inactive during many periods characterized by significantly high or low prices. These findings carry significant policy weight, particularly given the lack of transparency surrounding unit-level risk aversion and the visible risks involved in intervention decisions. Our study offers an analytical framework for evaluating concerns regarding risk aversion and provides a methodological template for investigating similar issues in other markets.

To simulate circulation, we apply a Froude number (Fr) of 0.1 (representing geostrophic flow), a Rossby number (Ro) of 0.1 (indicating quasi-geostrophic flow), and a Reynolds number (Re) of 10,000 (suggesting turbulent flow). Variations in circulation are induced by altering surface heating (via Newtonian cooling), Coriolis force (through rotation rate adjustments), and atmospheric thickness (by modifying the planet's gravitational acceleration). Results demonstrate that as the Coriolis force increases, the Froude number must be correspondingly raised to replicate Earth's observed monsoon-like circulation. Furthermore, we investigate how volcanic aerosols influence atmospheric transport, aerosol lifetime, and area-weighted mean temperatures under both current and elevated Coriolis conditions. Specifically, a planet with a 20% stronger Coriolis force exhibits a 2 K difference in mean surface temperature compared to Earth, alongside a 1.5-fold increase in aerosol lifetime. Furthermore, for the examined range of Coriolis strengths, we contend that the general circulation can be effectively represented as a rotating tank configuration, potentially enabling the simulation of million-ton atmospheric transport on exoplanets using laboratory-scale setups. We evaluate the carbon intensity of various training strategies on a complete ImageNet dataset (approximately 140TB). Specifically, the proposed algorithm is 2.7x more carbon-efficient than SSP and 6.3x more efficient than stochastic gradient learning (SGD). In terms of overall performance, the proposed method surpasses both the lowest and highest carbon-intensity baselines by 7.6% and 3.8%, respectively. These results suggest that the proposed AL strategy is a highly effective solution for labeling medium-scale data.

This paper introduces and evaluates an Adaptive Cooperative NOMA (ACN) protocol designed for vehicular communications at intersections.
