The paper addresses the simultaneous transmission of unicast data to multiple destinations and a common broadcast message using a multi-antenna base station (BS). Operating under a total power constraint, the associated optimization problem is generally difficult due to its non-convex nature and the lack of closed-form solutions. To address this, the broadcast power is first approximated by a continuous value, enabling the derivation of a high-performance closed-form solution for the unicast sub-problem. Following this, a low-complexity algorithm is proposed to fine-tune the approximate broadcast power for improved accuracy. Simulation results indicate that the total power consumption of the system follows a Gamma distribution. Leveraging this insight, the paper calculates the exact probability of successful broadcast delivery and the average number of successfully delivered unicast packets. The derived expressions are validated via Monte-Carlo simulations. The findings reveal that increasing the BS's number of antennas enhances both the exact and average numbers of successfully delivered packets. Additionally, adding antennas to the user equipment improves the average (but not the exact) number of successful deliveries. Finally, the accuracy of the proposed exact expressions is confirmed by comparing them with results from Monte-Carlo simulations.

This work investigates the wireless security of Intra-vehicle Communication Systems (ICS) employing Generalized Spatial Division Multiplexing (GSDM). Specifically, the optimal cutoff signal-to-interference-plus-noise

allows a single link to multiplex multiple spatial users by alternating transmission and reception in time. However, the optimal uplink/downlink division is influenced not only by the number of antennas but also by the count of simultaneous users, as adding more users increases the overhead for coherent combining. This paper derives the signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) for simple linear zero-forcing (ZF) as the user count varies. Based on this derivation, the optimal dual-link user distribution and corresponding ZF sine rates are analyzed under uniform and non-uniform Rayleigh fading conditions with direct line-of-sight (LOS). Numerical results compare the performance of maximum ratio transmission (MRT), optimal fixed dual-link user distributions, and optimal user distributions across different channel models. The findings reveal that for small user counts, fixed dual-link distributions can outperform dynamically optimized ones because the relative overhead of coherent combining is lower than interference. Conversely, as the user count grows, dynamically optimized dual-link user counts and sine rates can achieve the full multiplexing gain of a single-link system. For large user counts in direct LOS channels, the full multiplexing gain is no longer achievable due to the high combining overhead, yet the derived optimal user distributions and sine rates maximize system performance in such scenarios. Tarnopolski defined a family of $\mathbb{Z}_k$-extensible $\mathbb{Z}_3$-subfactors and derived a classification of their fusion rules; this family can also be viewed as a $\mathbb{Z}_k$-orbifold of the ADE subfactors. This subfactor invariant can likewise be defined utilizing 3-tensors. Under the assumption of the tensoriality conjecture, we show that this subfactor invariant is equivalent to the 3-tensors. In this study, we develop a novel stochastic hydrodynamic method within the positive-P phase-space framework specifically for interacting Bose gases. modes (PTMs) have been observed in the edge plasma of the JET tokamak. While PTMs are well-documented, their formation mechanisms remain poorly understood. Typically, PTMs, which are ELM-postcursors, are explained by magnetic field ergodization caused by edge localized modes and the subsequent development of a seed magnetic island into a PTM. This study proposes an alternative creation mechanism rooted in edge plasma turbulence concepts. A notable feature of ELM crashes is the abrupt discharge of a large portion of stored private plasma at the last flux surface between the separatrix and the q=1 rational surface. Based on this observation and drawing from turbulent plasma concepts, we define a specific plasma state for the crash phase where the edge plasma exhibits macroscopic turbulence. Consequently, the dissolution of stored plasma is attributed to turbulent transport. Notably, the intensity of this turbulence is sufficiently high to render the removal of a significant mass of plasma nearly instantaneous. Furthermore, we observe that the radius of the resulting hole in the density profile (defining the new pressure well for the inter-ELM phase) aligns closely with the scale length of the mode that would be formed if magnetic ergodization occurred. Therefore, we conclude that the magnetic scale of a PTM can be pre-defined by edge macroscopic turbulence. This new perspective offers a potential explanation for the variability in PTM sizes. Additionally, it clarifies why PTMs are not always present when a magnetic island is confirmed, as a localized structure is not necessarily created by magnetic ergodization. These modes are instead interpreted as a core plasma signature of the abrupt drop in density at the last flux surface during an ELM crash. Finally, we suggest that detecting PTMs implies that the edge plasma is not governed by turbulent transport in the same manner as the bulk plasma. Instead, it possesses a localized structure with a size determined by a mechanism that can be initialized by, yet distinct from, a magnetic island. We propose that this structure is likely produced by a combination of two effects: magnetic island formation and any localized localization mechanism for turbulent eddies.

Collision evasion maneuvers are formulated using dynamic vortex potential fields (PFs) and their negative gradients, creating a reciprocal, cooperative dynamic between the robots. The repulsive field depends on the relative velocity and position of a robot with respect to others, and the inclusion of vorticity in its definition ensures there are no local minima. This field activates only when a robot is on a trajectory that could lead to a collision with other mobile robots or stationary obstacles. Through an analysis of kinematics-based engagement dynamics, the study defines the safe region and capture area; the safe region is where the PF does not localize, while the capture area is where it does. To guarantee safe collision-avoidance movements, the paper derives conditions for the capture area based on the maximum force a robot can exert, the PF's decay exponent, and the initial relative velocity and position. Specifically, the study focuses on collisions occurring at constant speeds, classifying such events into three scenarios based on the initial relative velocity: head-on collision, tail-on collision, and oblique collision. It is demonstrated that in both head-on and tail-on collision cases, the PF's capture area extends infinitely. Furthermore, specific conditions governing oblique collisions at constant speeds are established. When an robot starts outside the capture area, a safe maneuver is guaranteed; conversely, if the robot is within the capture area, a safe maneuver is not guaranteed, and the field may localize. Additionally, necessary and sufficient conditions for the field to localize are derived, indicating that a collision occurs once a local minimum is reached. Finally, the efficacy of the proposed method in ensuring collision avoidance is validated through computer simulations and experimental tests involving real Holon-2 robots. Collision outcomes on a real platform are successfully averted by setting an appropriate threshold for the PF's maximum force. Furthermore, a performance metric is introduced to quantify and compare the effectiveness of collision-avoidance movements under various conditions. This metric, applicable to both non-holonomic and holonomic robots, quantifies the change in the robot's trajectory. Simulation results show that the path length increased by up to 60% in head-on and tail-on scenarios and decreased by up to 30% in oblique collisions compared to a reference length. On the holonomic platform, the path length varied by up to 90% across different collision types. Composed of passive reflective elements, an IRS can adjust the phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization of incident waveforms. These advantageous properties enable the control and optimization of wireless channel characteristics to meet specific signal design and processing requirements, thereby offering substantial potential for radar applications. Although IRS has been shown to enhance radar performance by improving target detectability and increasing precision, its integration into wireless systems remains in an early research phase. This work introduces a practical IRS design for radar enhancement that operates without a connected transceiver. In this Intelligent Reflecting Surface for Radar (IRS-R) setup, the transmitter directly sends a signal to the IRS, which reflects it toward the target. The received signal at the radar results from the combination of direct and reflected propagation paths. This paper presents the joint optimization of the transmitting signal and the IRS configuration (including amplitude and phase coefficients) for single-target detection and estimation. Since the channel linking the IRS to the target is typically unknown, we employ a robust optimization framework. Our proposed approach is validated both numerically and experimentally. Numerical results compare our method with direct transmission and channel-based optimization, while experimental findings illustrate the improvement in radar detectability caused by the IRS. Both findings demonstrate that our proposed robust optimization effectively enhances radar performance even when target channel information is unknown or poorly estimated. This research opens avenues for future integration of IRS into wireless systems. Notably, our experimental results confirm that optimal IRS coefficients can be determined through reinforcement learning. This conclusion supports the feasibility of utilizing machine learning for IRS optimization in practical wireless communication scenarios. First, we review the related work on IRS-R for radar. ing software vulnerabilities. Although significant advancements have been made recently, accurately measuring and comparing the efficacy of different fuzzers remains an unresolved research challenge. In software testing, mutation analysis stands as the gold standard for assessing test quality; it evaluates a test's capacity to identify synthetic bugs, operating on the principle that tests failing to catch these artificial faults will also miss real ones. By encompassing various coverage metrics and offering a vast, diverse array of faults that can be engineered to be difficult to trigger and detect, mutation analysis effectively avoids issues related to saturation and overfitting. However, traditional mutation analysis is prohibitively expensive for fuzzing because each mutation requires independent evaluation. This paper leverages modern mutation analysis techniques that pool multiple mutations, enabling the first-ever evaluation and comparison of fuzzers using this method. We introduce a dedicated benchmark for fuzzers, applying it to several popular tools and targets. Our comprehensive study demonstrates how this approach allows for the assessment of fuzzer performance and the measurement of improvements in specific techniques. Although our findings indicate that current fuzzers detect only a small fraction of mutations, we view this as a critical area for future research, specifically focusing on enhancing (1) the detection of failures beyond generic crashes and (2) the ability to trigger mutations (and consequently, faults). Ultimately, we hope this work offers a robust framework for evaluating fuzzers that can be readily adapted to assess emerging techniques.

Modern program testing methods that rely on feedback, such as fuzzing and program synthesis, benefit significantly from incorporating program mutators. These components, however, remain largely underutilized and lack deep integration. We introduce LibFuzzerWithMutations, an extension of LibFuzzer that embeds program mutators directly into the fuzzing cycle. This extension supports both white-box and gray-box approaches: for white-box fuzzing, the mutator attempts to execute control flow changes induced by mutated inputs, while for gray-box fuzzing, it tries to provoke these changes via side-channel instrumentation. Unlike previous methods that could only induce and detect a single mutation per target, our approach supports programs with multiple, simultaneously active mutations. To validate the feasibility of this approach, we developed a white-box variant and a matching gray-box variant, along with a benchmark suite of modification-sensitive bugs. Our results show that the white-box version succeeds in triggering and detecting approximately 75% of changes in a medium-scale dataset, and roughly 90% of mutations in a smaller, carefully selected dataset. Conversely, the gray-box version failed to trigger any mutations across all cases

Many of these methods rely on mechanisms applied to pre-trained representations, restricting or entirely avoiding updates to the backbone during continual training. In this paper, we challenge the necessity of such model complexity for achieving high performance by introducing a simple baseline that utilizes layer-free learning rules with a pretrained initializer. Our method, named Layer-free Initializer based Sequential Learning (LASER), is equally simple as the baseline. Experimental results show that LASER surpasses the baseline and various state-of-the-art techniques across both image and object recognition benchmarks. Additionally, we establish a set of guidelines for setting up a strong LASER baseline, which, when incorporated, yields even stronger outcomes. The code for both the baseline and LASER is available on GitHub.

We address a critical gap in current literature regarding bounds and guidelines for selecting hyperparameters for complex continual learning architectures. This work proposes a straightforward method to determine learning rates and other hyperparameters automatically. Our proposed LASER requires no manual tuning beyond the hyperparameters already inherent in its pretrained initializer. LASER exceeds state-of-the-art continuation performance on multiple classification benchmarks, including a toy 10-way 50-class problem, a 20-way 200-class image classification task (ImageNet-C), and an object recognition task (Objects 365). Furthermore, we demonstrate that LASER performs as well as, or better than, 30 other state-of-the-art algorithms on the Trecal evaluation server for the Continual Learning and Evaluation Competition (CLEVAL) 2021. Code for LASER and the baseline can be found on GitHub.

We present a method for automatically determining hyperparameters, such as learning rates, for sophisticated continual learning models without requiring manual adjustment. Our proposed LASER initializes complex networks using pretrained models but requires no further fine-tuning beyond the hyperparameters already specified in those initializations. Shmaya defined $\lambda$-Lipschitz games, where each player's payoff function exhibits $\lambda$-Lipschitz continuity relative to other players' actions. They demonstrated that these games possess $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria under specific conditions for $\epsilon$ and $\lambda$, but they did not address the computational difficulty of locating such equilibria. This paper addresses that gap by constructing a query-efficient reduction from broader game classes to Lipschitz games. Utilizing this reduction, we establish an exponential query lower bound for any randomized algorithm seeking $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria in $n$-player, binary-action, $\lambda$-Lipschitz games, where the exponent scales with $\frac{n\lambda}{\epsilon}$. Furthermore, we propose "Multi-Lipschitz games," a generalization allowing player-specific Lipschitz constants, and demonstrate a reduction to standard Lipschitz games, revealing that the critical parameter is the sum of individual Lipschitz values. Finally, we derive an exponential lower bound on the deterministic query complexity required to find $\epsilon$-approximate correlated equilibria in $n$-player, $m$-action, $\lambda$-Lipschitz games for sufficiently large $\epsilon$, thereby highlighting the necessity of randomized approaches for the aforementioned results. # Reliable Parameter Tuning via Dataset Scaling

K-fold cross-validation (CV) is a common framework for assessing machine learning models, essential for estimating performance, selecting algorithms, and guiding parameter tuning. However, because K-fold CV involves random data splitting, it introduces stochasticity that can severely impact performance estimates and lead to unreliable tuning outcomes. Current solutions for datasets up to a few hundred thousand items rely on smoothing these estimates, but such methods fail when scaling to larger data volumes. We establish a theoretical framework analyzing the strengths and limitations of existing approaches, which are often constrained to specific model classes or moderate dataset sizes. Our work inspires a solution utilizing a optimal parameter search space derived from an information theoretic lower bound on estimator variance. We demonstrate that combining this bound with a Poisson approximation of scaled data enables efficient hyperparameter tuning. We validate these findings on multiple models across various datasets, observing improvements in performance estimates that are critical for both theoretical modeling and practical applications. Code for all experiments can be found at https://github.com/hshahar/cv-scaling.

To overcome this challenge, Teacher-Student architectures were introduced, enabling compact student models to match the performance of parameter-heavy teacher models. Recently, these models have seen widespread adoption in various fields, yet they often rely on dense connections that create significant latency and power overheads during inference, making edge deployment difficult. We introduce a "generalized pair hopping" framework capable of emulating the Hamiltonans for ultracold atomic gases in undecorated and decorated optical lattices, as well as for Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya stabilized bilayer quantum magnets. In this model, two coupled lattice sites are treated as a single effective site; the exchange coupling and interaction energies are determined by the overlap and interaction of the ground states of the two-site units. **Approach:** Continuous k-space data were collected using a rewound Cartesian acquisition with spiral profile ordering (rCASPR). This method was designed to match the contrast of conventional linear phase encoding while organizing data into multiple respiratory phases. Low-resolution, respiratory-correlated 4D images were reconstructed via compressed sensing to estimate non-rigid deformation vector fields, which facilitated motion-compensated image reconstruction. The rCASPR sampling technique was compared against linear and CASPR sampling regarding point-spread function (PSF) and image contrast through in silico, phantom, and in vivo studies. A grid search was employed to determine optimal reconstruction parameters for low-resolution 4D-MRI, specifically spatial resolution and temporal regularization. The proposed motion-compensated rCASPR was tested in eight healthy volunteers and benchmarked against free-breathing scans utilizing linear sampling, with image quality assessed both visually and quantitatively using gradient entropy.

**Findings:** rCASPR demonstrated a superior PSF (comparable in ky but narrower in kz) with no significant difference in image contrast relative to linear sampling. Optimal 4D-MRI reconstruction parameters were identified as a spatial resolution of $4.5 \text{ mm}^3$ and a temporal regularization of $0.016 \text{ mm}^{-1} r^{-1}$. rCASPR yielded motion-compensated 4D images that exhibited clearer anatomical details and well-defined lung boundaries compared to their linear sampling counterparts. In healthy volunteers, rCASPR produced significantly better visual and quantitative image quality than linear sampling.

**Conclusion:** rCASPR maintains the same image contrast as linear sampling but offers a shorter scan duration with equivalent image quality. Consequently, rCASPR represents a promising method for acquiring high-resolution, motion-compensated 4D-MRI data from free-breathing patients.

This paper examines domain representations through CF-approximation spaces, introducing the concepts of CF-approximation spaces and CF-closed sets. It is demonstrated that the collection of CF-closed sets within a CF-approximation space, when ordered by set inclusion, forms a continuous domain, and conversely, every continuous domain is isomorphic to the family of CF-closed sets of some such space. Furthermore, CF-approximable relations are defined via a categorical approach, which enables the proof that the category of CF-approximation spaces and CF-approximable relations is equivalent to the category of continuous domains and Scott-continuous maps. Additionally, the complete lattice of CF-closed sets over a CF-approximation space corresponds to the image of the canonical embedding of the Scott domain associated with the CPO of lower powersets derived from the CF-approximable relation. Finally, the paper explores the connection between CF-approximable relations and domain morphisms, revealing that the category of CF-approximation spaces and morphisms is equivalent to the category of Scott domains and their morphisms, and admissible morphisms, respectively. In this Part II, we establish that these geometries allow for surgery-style arguments to remove the singular sets. As a consequence, we prove the following theorem:

**Theorem 1.1 (See Theorem 4.1 for the precise statement).** *Let $M^n$, where $n \geq 5$, be a compact manifold equipped with a metric of positive scalar curvature, and let $\Sigma^n \subset M^n$ minimize area within its homology class. Then, $\Sigma^n$ must be embedded.*

This result constitutes a significant generalization of Priori [8], which addressed the case where $M^n = \mathbb{R}^3 \setminus \{p_1, \dots, p_k\}$. Our proof relies on the criteria for pinching the second fundamental form developed in [5]. Specifically, if the $C^2$ norm of the scalar curvature of $\Sigma^n$ remains bounded, then the fundamental form can be controlled via the use of covering maps [7]. Otherwise, the singular set of $\Sigma^n$ can be addressed through the results established in [5]. Notably, the methods presented in [5] are applicable to singular varifolds as well. Consequently, the proof of Theorem 1.1 remains valid under the additional assumption that the singular set of $\Sigma^n$ is empty varifold-wise. We observe that prior to our work, no surgery arguments had been formulated for singular objects. Since the completion of this paper, a related result has been published [10]; however, the specific details of that work do not overlap with ours.

In the special case where $M^n = \mathbb{R}^3 \setminus \{p_1, \dots, p_k\}$, the theorem was previously established by Priori [8] and Soreti [9]. The connection between these results and the general case is fully detailed in [5].

Aggregators manage large volumes of distributed, controllable loads for end-users and can inject or absorb power to support the electric grid during stress. Their value lies in relieving bottlenecks on transmission and distribution lines, supporting voltage, and balancing supply and demand. To do this, operators (like ISO-NE or regional utilities) or auxiliary systems (such as primary frequency response) send price or signal incentives to aggregators, who then coordinate individual loads. Rising inflation rates have driven individuals to shift funds from savings into stocks, commodities, and other investment avenues. Deep Learning models have recently demonstrated remarkable success in predictive tasks, inspiring researchers to apply these techniques to investment analysis. This study utilizes the Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE) to assess the performance of our proposed approach. The market's stock direction is crucial for investors, as accurate direction prediction is a fundamental yet challenging task. While various methods exist for forecasting stock direction, technical analysis remains the most prominent. Each stock possesses unique technical indicators, and no single stock follows an identical direction pattern. Given the vast array of technical analysis methods, it is impossible to predict every stock's direction using a single model. To address this, we trained multiple models with different features and combined their outputs to predict stock direction. This paper introduces a novel technique for forecasting stock direction. Our proposed method employs a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to predict daily stock direction. Furthermore, we developed a new feature named Market Sentiment (MS), which captures the sentiment surrounding a stock to aid prediction. The MS feature integrates several technical indicators, making it a unique addition to existing technical analysis methods. Finally, an Ensemble Learning (EL) strategy was implemented to predict stock direction using three models and the EL strategy, and this approach proved effective. The main contributions of this work are: (1) introducing the new MS feature, and (2) developing an EL strategy for predicting stock direction. Empirical results indicate that our proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques.

intruder with length $L$ and diameter $D$ moving through water-saturated granular beds at a fixed depth. Using polystyrene and hydrogel grains with diameter $d$, we examine materials exhibiting high and negligible contact friction, respectively. Drag forces were measured for orientations both perpendicular ($F_\perp$) and parallel ($F_\parallel$) to the cylinder's axis across a range of speeds $U$, spanning both inertial and quasi-static regimes. Results indicate that the drag anisotropy ratio, $R = F_\perp/F_\parallel$, is strongly influenced by both the internal friction angle of the grains and the relative size between the intruder and the grains. Specifically, for small intruders ($D/d < 1$) with high friction materials, $R$ is substantially larger than for large intruders ($D/d > 1$) with low friction materials. Furthermore, $R$ exhibits only minor variation with depth and remains largely independent of material friction when the intruder is large. Parallel drag $F_\parallel$ aligns with slender-body theory for both small and large $D/d$ ratios. Finally, we analyze the dominant physical mechanisms driving these drag forces in both orientation regimes within inertial and quasi-static limits. Notably, in the quasi-static regime, $R$ rises sharply with increasing $U$, offering direct evidence of an axis switch phenomenon where $R < 1$ at higher velocities. Our observations regarding the orientation dependence of drag in slender bodies consistent with slender-body theory for both directions may provide valuable insights for enhancing the efficiency of biofouling control systems. These comparisons yield disc properties, such as gas surface density ($\Sigma_{\rm H_2}$), that vary by orders of magnitude. Specifically, we find that: (1) mean values of $\Sigma_{\rm H_2}$ in the outer discs are $>5.5\times$ lower than those near the nuclei; (2) a significant fraction of outer discs are resolved at the 500~pc scale, whereas most nuclei and their immediate surroundings are not; and (3) a corresponding fraction of outside-on IR luminosity is derived from these 500~pc scale discs. These results indicate that merging galaxies like Arp 220 and Mrk 274 are composed of a collection of diverse disc systems. We suggest that the wide range of densities found in these objects may help explain the wide range of densities observed in isolated star-forming discs. Furthermore, we note that the wide density range between the outside-on nuclei and their associated discs, along with the wide range of densities within the discs themselves, may assist in explaining the wide range of dust processing environments observed in LIRCs and ULIRCs. Finally, we observe that the wide density range between outside-on discs and their central black holes may help explain why most ULIRCs exhibit hard power-law AGN spectra, regardless of redshift. These findings support the view that the complex nuclear emission in LIRCs and ULIRCs can be attributed to a superposition of many small, self-gravitating discs of varying sizes and densities, rather than a single, monolithic disc. Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO) has recently addressed these issues by employing probabilistic models; however, its adoption has been limited by the complexity of constructing these models. SBO typically accelerates convergence by decomposing the parameter space using contextual insights from system experts. We introduce BoAnon, an SBO framework that automatically learns decomposition structures from diverse contextual knowledge. BoAnon offers a modular architecture that seamlessly integrates various probabilistic models, enabling an automated learning process that acquires decomposition structures and contextual effects simultaneously. Evaluations on cluster scheduling systems show that BoAnon achieves performance comparable to hand-crafted SBO methods but across a 5x larger search space. We address the problem of scheduling independent jobs on a cluster to maximize resource utilization and overall performance. Our solution, BANON, utilizes Bayesian optimization with noise-only neural networks. Banon automatically infers interaction patterns among cluster resources by analyzing historical job executions, thereby accelerating scheduling optimization and reducing the number of evaluations needed. In experiments on Google's internal production cluster, Banon achieved significant improvements in both resource utilization and job performance over current auto-tuning systems. Specifically, Banon outperformed existing schedulers in resource utilization across all tested search spaces. When evaluating multi-dimensional search spaces, BoAnon was roughly 3x more efficient than state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, in single-machine algorithm acceleration tasks, BoAnon was about 6x more efficient than LightBO, another recent Bayesian optimization framework.

we investigated the connection between initial geometric anisotropy and anisotropic flow in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 200 GeV. Our results show that, unlike the elliptic flow $v_2$, the triangular flow $v_3$ exhibits minimal dependence on centrality. Once the influence of initial geometry is accounted for, the ratio $v_3/\epsilon_3$ rises with increasing transverse particle density, mirroring the behavior of $v_2/\epsilon_2$. Furthermore, the $p_T$ dependence of $v_3$ observed across identified particles follows a qualitative pattern similar to that of $v_2$. However, the magnitude of $v_3$ derived from our model exceeds current experimental measurements, a discrepancy that becomes more pronounced at higher transverse momenta and for identified particles. We attribute this overestimation of $v_3$ to the explicit geometry effects incorporated within the AMPT framework. Additionally, the sensitivity of the $p_T$ dependence of $v_3$ to the interconversion between quarks and hadrons suggests that hadronization via the hadron cascade process may offer a potential probe of quantum chromodynamics in the non-perturbative regime. Finally, we offer a qualitative qualitative interpretation of the system-size dependence of $v_3/\epsilon_3$. processes can be effectively modeled using specific parametric frameworks to facilitate statistical analysis. However, standard maximum likelihood (ML) estimation and inference techniques are often fragile, lacking robustness against minor model misspecifications or data contamination. While non-parametric alternatives offer robustness, they frequently suffer from a significant loss in efficiency. To address this, we propose a robust parameter estimation method for discretely observed data from parametric stochastic processes, leveraging the advantageous properties of the density power divergence within a minimum distance inference framework. Specifically, we introduce minimum density power divergence estimators (MDPDE) tailored for independent increment and Markov processes. We derive asymptotic consistency and distributional properties for these MDPDEs under dependent stochastic process settings and demonstrate their superiority over conventional ML estimators through examples such as Poisson processes, drifted Brownian motion, and autoregressive models. Furthermore, we display the practical utility of MDPDEs in statistical process control. The analysis is made possible by the computational power of the R package `robustmarkov`.

Stochastic processes are widely utilized to model evolving phenomena in fields like genomics, finance, and quality control. Although often assumed to follow specific parametric models, it is crucial to develop parameter estimation methods that remain reliable even when these assumptions are slightly violated. This paper presents a class of robust estimators for discretely sampled stochastic processes, with a specific focus on those featuring independent increments or the Markov property. Utilizing the density power divergence, we demonstrate that our proposed estimators maintain robustness across various applications and show improved performance in parameter estimation and hypothesis testing for underlying drifts, particularly in the presence of outlying observations.

Parametric estimation via maximum likelihood (ML) is highly efficient but lacks robustness, making it sensitive to outliers and minor model violations. Consequently, there is a pressing need for methods that preserve efficiency while enhancing robustness. This research investigates such methods for inference on stochastic processes. Consider a sequence of observations $X_0, X_1, \dots, X_n$ from a Markov process $\{X_k : k=0,1, \dots \}$ on a state space $S$. Our analysis of electron temperature distributions in active galaxies reveals values ranging from 8,000 to over 30,000 K. In Mrk 79 and Mrk 348, gas outflows generate shocks that significantly influence the observed temperature patterns, whereas standard photoionization models adequately explain the temperature data for Mrk 607. For Mrk 79 and Mrk 348, we identify direct evidence of shock-ionization oriented orthogonally to the ionization axis; these shocks are readily detectable because the nuclear dusty torus shields the AGN radiation field. This observation further suggests that even when ionization cones are narrow, associated shocks can exhibit much wider angular extents. However, the resource constraints, unpredictable communication channels, and fluctuating operational environments inherent to IoT create substantial challenges for software vendors during application testing. While various emulators are available for IoT system testing, they suffer from several drawbacks, including insufficient support for logical dependencies and sophisticated fault injection, the need for manual behavior validation, and a narrow focus on specific platforms or languages. To overcome these shortcomings, we introduce Frisbee, a framework designed for the automated testing of IoT applications. Frisbee streamlines the testing workflow by facilitating the rapid deployment of distributed virtual testbeds via Kubernetes and enabling the definition of "what-if" scenarios that combine intricate sequences of workloads and fault injections. We assessed Frisbee's utility and efficacy by applying it to the fault tolerance testing of an IoT-based health monitoring system. The results demonstrate that Frisbee can significantly reduce testing time and lower the cost per test compared to existing emulators or manual testing methods. Implementations of our evaluations are accessible at https://frisbee-testbed.github.io/. To accompany these experiments, we have also released a set of Jupyter notebooks available at https://github.com/mirsharify/425F-Project. By offering a tool for exploring various testing strategies, Frisbee aims to assist researchers and practitioners in effectively developing and testing software for distributed and real-time embedded systems. We invite contributions to improve the Frisbee framework, and we are open to media coverage or inclusion in textbook/course collections.

Current approaches typically place agents into scenes based on manual heuristics, which restricts their capacity to capture the genuine complexity and variety of actual traffic, thereby creating a content disparity between synthetic and real environments. Consequently, existing simulators fail to achieve the fidelity required for training and evaluating autonomous vehicles. To overcome this, we introduce SceneGen, a neural autoregressive model that operates without relying on rules or heuristics. Specifically, provided with the ego-vehicle's state and a high-definition map of the surroundings, SceneGen populates the scene with diverse actor classes and synthesizes their dimensions, orientations, and velocities. We demonstrate on two extensive datasets that SceneGen can accurately model the distributions found in real traffic. Furthermore, we show that combining SceneGen with sensor simulation enables the training of perception models that effectively generalize to real-world conditions. In particular, we utilize this setup to develop a system capable of driving through diverse real-world intersections. Finally, we discuss limitations of our method and propose directions for future research. Code can be found at https://github.com/kailash-k/SceneGen.

This paper introduces a novel family of second-order, fourth-order, and super-high-order compact difference schemes designed to preserve the minimum-entropy solution for total variation diminishing (TVD) shock-capturing schemes applied to the scalar conservation law of entropy. The analysis demonstrates that, unlike most existing compact difference schemes which preserve the full entropy solution, these schemes can effectively mitigate the entropy violation found in the total variation of the time derivative ($TV_y(u(y,\cdot))$) for a fixed spatial location $y$ and $t>0$. When applied to a linear advection equation, these schemes result in implicit schemes with characteristic equations composed of multiple harmonic components. Consequently, they can be regarded as compact versions of multi-order compact schemes previously defined for the heat equation. Numerical experiments highlight the superiority of these schemes in capturing shocks and resolving discontinuities. Furthermore, the scheme exhibits super-high-order accuracy, with its practical application supported by its ability to preserve the minimum-entropy solution. It is important to note that because these schemes are implicit, they can only be applied to nonlinear scalar conservation laws where an explicit entropy fix exists; a significant example is the Burgers' equation. However, for scalar conservation laws lacking an explicit entropy fix, the issue of entropy violation remains an open challenge. These schemes are particularly beneficial for TVD compact shock-capturing schemes of order three or lower. Just as the standard Lax-Wendroff method is a limited version of the fourth-order Runge-Kutta scheme, these schemes can be extended to all standard schemes of order four and lower, as well as to many high-order schemes. Specifically, extensions include compact versions of the Runge-Kutta 4th order scheme, the Shu-Osher scheme, and the Deng-Zhang scheme. A primary advantage of these schemes is their ability to reduce errors associated with entropy violation in the spatial variable $y$ by approximately two to four times compared to their corresponding standard schemes. Additionally, these schemes significantly enhance the accuracy of shocks and discontinuities in solutions to the Burgers' equation. It is anticipated that these schemes will find broad applications in shock-capturing schemes for other time-dependent PDEs that possess conservation laws or other crucial properties. We also expect them to be valuable for finite difference time domain (FDTD) methods used in electromagnetic field simulations. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for joint ergodicity that are sufficiently adaptable to encompass the majority of established examples of such sequences while also addressing several related open questions. A notable aspect of our methodology is its reliance on techniques developed by Peluse and Prendiville, adapted to an ergodic context, thereby circumventing the deep ergodic theory tools previously required for similar proofs. This approach primarily facilitates the derivation of quantitative variants for the finitary version of the polynomial Szemerédi theorem. A central component of our work are novel applications of the general transverse structure theorem, which we also utilize in related research. Additionally, we provide references linking our findings to recent advancements by Peluse and Prendiville. A significant innovation of our strategy is the early employment of the pointwise ergodic theorem, which allows us to avoid the quantitative challenges inherent in later applications of the maximum density lemma. These results have been presented without dependence on the more recent work of Peluse and Prendiville. Furthermore, we address several issues arising from an earlier draft that utilized prior techniques different from our current methodology.

We examine the link between two concepts defining the "quantitative" version of the polynomial Hahn–Banach theorem: one formulated via approximate factorization and the other using shattering. Our main finding demonstrates that these two statements are equivalent. This relationship yields a refined, quantitative form of the polynomial Riesz representation theorem. Additionally, we provide a quantitative variant of a result by Peluse and Prendiville, specifically their quantitative version of the polynomial Szemerédi theorem. We also note that our methods offer a new proof for the main conclusion of Peluse and Prendiville. Finally, we illustrate how our findings yield a quantitative version of the "folklore" result stating that if a set of integers is jointly ergodic, then it is ergodic with respect to all polynomials. Previously, this implication was proven directly, as the two forms of joint ergodicity are equivalent. Prior to our work, it was an open question whether the two formulations of the quantitative polynomial Hahn–Banach theorem were equivalent. We clarify that our findings do not depend on the recent findings of Peluse and Prendiville.

tracking the evolution of superbubbles driven by stellar winds and supernovae from young, coeval massive star clusters situated within low-metallicity ($Z = 0.02$Z$_{\odot}$), clumpy molecular clouds. The investigation focuses on the early phases of superbubble development, specifically examining pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae events. The primary objectives are to analyze dust grain growth within orbiting dusty clumps and the swept-up supershell of the superbubble, as well as to assess the survival of dust grains generated by sequential supernovae. The models incorporate the gravitational potential of the star cluster, the self-gravity of the parent cloud, radiative cooling (including dust-induced processes), and a sophisticated population synthesis model for the coeval cluster. Consistent with previous findings, superbubbles embedded in clumpy media become significantly distorted, expanding predominantly through low-density channels via hot gas streaming. Results for massive ($\sim10^7$M$_{\odot}$) molecular clouds hosting a super star cluster ($\sim5.6\times10^5$M$_{\odot}$) indicate that grain growth increases dust mass at a rate of $\sim4.8\times10^{-5}$M$_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$ during the first 2.5 Myr. Meanwhile, the net dust contribution from pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae remains negligible after these initial 2.5 Myr because the rapidly collapsing, dust-filled superbubble destroys the fragile grains produced by the first supernova. However, if the medium is segment into thinner, denser layers, a larger fraction of dust generated by the first supernova can survive, potentially resulting in a net dust mass increase during the early superbubble phase. These outcomes provide a fresh perspective on the origins of dust in massive galaxies and luminous infrared galaxies during the star-forming epochs following the early universe. Additional conclusions regarding the creation of super shells and ionized bubbles around young star clusters are also presented. Finally, these results align with a previous statistical analysis of observational data on superbubbles (or super shells) caused by star clusters, which indicated a net mass increase for dust along the line of sight. These findings offer an alternative explanation to the recently suggested meandering process for this mass increase. (Far3Det), which targets objects located beyond a specific range, such as greater than 50 meters. This capability is critical for autonomous vehicles (AVs) traveling at highway speeds, as detecting distant obstacles is essential for maintaining adequate braking distances. However, existing AV benchmarks like nuScenes largely overlook this challenge by restricting performance evaluation to distances within 50 meters. This limitation stems partly from the difficulty of generating far-field 3D annotations, especially for LiDAR sensors, which often yield sparse point returns for distant objects; our analysis reveals that nearly 50% of objects beyond 50 meters have zero LiDAR points. Additionally, current 3D detection metrics apply uniform tolerance thresholds to both near and far objects, a "one-size-fits-all" approach that contradicts the varying tolerances inherent in human vision and stereo disparity. These factors result in an incomplete assessment of Far3Det. For instance, despite the conventional belief that high-resolution RGB sensors are crucial for detecting distant objects, LiDAR-based methods currently outperform RGB counterparts on standard benchmark leaderboards. As an initial step toward a dedicated Far3Det benchmark, we identified well-annotated scenes within the nuScenes dataset to create a robust far-field validation set. We also introduced a new evaluation protocol and tested various 3D detection methods specifically for this task. Our findings strongly validate the established wisdom that high-resolution RGB significantly enhances far-field detection performance, establishing RGB methods as the new leaders. Notably, our best model, Far3Det, achieves an average improvement of over 25% across all evaluation criteria compared to current state-of-the-art solutions. Lastly, we emphasized the necessity of specialized loss functions and multi-scale training to successfully address Far3Det. All source code and models are accessible via GitHub.

We introduce TSHNet, a novel framework for multi-object 3D detection in LiDAR data that utilizes point-based features and Set Hierarchical Network blocks. The core concept is to model the point cloud of each object as a distinct point set to enhance feature expression, while simultaneously leveraging the complementary information from surrounding points to improve the features of object points. TSHNet achieves an mAP of 23.0% and a junction detection score (JDS) of 12.3% on the nuScenes dataset, significantly surpassing the current state-of-the-art Far3Det methods. However, acquiring this data is challenging because sampling numerous ground states across a high-dimensional PES often demands an extensive number of state preparations. This study introduces a generative quantum machine learning framework designed to generate quantum states at any specified location on the PES. The model is trained on a discrete set of ground states and capable of preparing them with high fidelity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that training the network via reinforcement learning significantly enhances its performance. To validate these findings, we prepared ground states for the H$_4$ and CO$_2$ molecules across various molecular configurations. Our results indicate that a minimally parameterized neural quantum state (NQS) can effectively evaluate the PES for small to medium-sized molecules, outperforming traditional parameterized estimators like quantum neural networks (QNNs) in this specific context. Although generative machine learning for quantum state preparation has been explored previously, this work represents one of the first demonstrations that such approaches can be viable for chemical applications. This technique may facilitate the accurate determination of molecular properties, including reaction rates and proton affinity, that rely on the relative energy surface. Ultimately, this approach could be integrated with quantum algorithms for computing electron proton matrix elements, thereby improving chemical simulations both on classical systems and quantum devices. Introduction: The relative potential energy surface (PES), which maps energy as a function of nuclear coordinates, is essential for understanding chemical reactions derived from first principles. While the Born-Oppenheimer approximation enables the calculation of this surface by determining the ground state of the electronic Hamiltonian for various nuclear configurations, the high dimensionality of the problem hinders the acquisition of complete PES data. Although scaling laws suggest that classical full configuration interaction (FCI) can solve small systems and approximate FCI for larger systems with multi-reference methods, the high dimensionality of the PES presents a significant sampling challenge. Even with the support of high-performance computing (HPC) resources, obtaining a relative PES for a single molecule requires calculating the ground state across a vast number of sampled nuclear states. While the FCI method is exact, it becomes computationally prohibitive when applied to multiple nuclear configurations, as the computational cost scales factorially with the total number of electrons. To address this difficulty, we propose employing quantum state preparation (QSP) and machine learning to prepare the ground state of a molecular Hamiltonian at any given nuclear configuration. soft-tissue navigation, specifically within laparoscopic liver surgery. This process involves aligning a preoperative CT-derived organ model with an intraoperative surface reconstructed from laparoscopic video. The task is complex due to factors such as sparse and noisy real-time data, numerous unknowns regarding tissue properties and boundary conditions, and the difficulty of establishing correspondences between pre- and intraoperative datasets. These challenges are exacerbated by the liver's lack of distinct surface features and the disparate noise characteristics of the imaging modalities used. To address this, we developed a convolutional neural network that simultaneously performs surface correspondence search and non-rigid registration. The network was trained on physically accurate biomechanical simulations of randomly generated, deforming organ-like structures, enabling immediate generalization to new patients without retraining. By incorporating varying levels of noise into the intraoperative surfaces during training, the model achieves robustness against noisy data. During inference, the network generates a displacement field that aligns the preoperative volume with the partial intraoperative surface. Experimental results demonstrate that the approach effectively translates to real-world data while maintaining high inference speed, and the source code is publicly available. This method facilitates forward navigation, allowing for the projection of anatomical features from a 3D organ model onto the operating room camera. We anticipate that this contact-free technique will enhance safety and efficiency in laparoscopic liver procedures.

**Summary6**: We introduce a deep learning approach for forward non-rigid registration, simultaneously predicting correspondence and aligning images. The method learns from physically based simulations of soft tissues, requiring no hyperparameter tuning at inference. It handles noisy data, generalizes to new cases immediately, and supports iterative forward registration to match the reliability of traditional techniques.

Although recent advancements have been made in deformable medical image alignment, these methods often struggle with two key issues: (1) a reliance on hand-crafted feature descriptors and displacement fields that require optimization, and (2) an inability to accurately handle partial volume data. This paper presents a novel framework that overcomes these limitations.

We propose a new approach to partial deformable registration that utilizes physically based biomechanical simulation. Unlike prior methods, our framework avoids the need for hyperparameter optimization, ensuring immediate generalization to unseen data. To validate the model's applicability to real patient data, we evaluated it on both synthetic datasets and CT scans from a prostate ablation study.

Our findings indicate that the proposed method is feasible for clinical use, potentially offering several advantages over current state-of-the-art solutions.

While these vectors are highly valuable for subsequent tasks like collision avoidance and action recognition, acquiring precise annotations for LiDAR and stereo camera data is both laborious and computationally expensive. To overcome this annotation barrier, we propose a solution on two fronts: a new 3D scene flow benchmark and a novel self-supervised training framework. The benchmark comprises datasets structured to evaluate flow estimation across increasing levels of complexity, ranging from isolated moving objects to complex real-world scenes. Additionally, we introduce Adversarial Metric Learning for self-supervised flow estimation. In this setup, a primary model estimates flow from sequences of point clouds, while a secondary model learns a latent metric to differentiate between the flow-translated points and the target point cloud. This latent metric is optimized using a Multi-Scale Triplet loss that incorporates intermediary feature vectors. By applying our benchmark, we analyzed baseline and proposed model performances, discovering that our approach effectively maintains motion coherence and local geometry preservation—capabilities often lacking in other self-supervised methods. However, handling occlusions remains an unresolved challenge. Overall, our approach achieves comparable or superior results to existing methods on several metrics without relying on annotated flow data, demonstrating robustness across diverse scene types and complex configurations. We released the benchmark and all code on GitHub to encourage further research into self-supervised learning for 3D flow estimation. We contend that our method and benchmark establish a robust foundation for future evaluations of 3D scene flow estimation. This work extends the limitations of prior approaches in occlusion handling and scene complexity.

This research explores the thermodynamic behavior of spin-polarized strange quark matter (SQM) at non-zero temperatures under the influence of a strong magnetic field, based on the MIT bag model. Consequently, we determine the spin-polarized state equation and investigate the formation of spin-polarized quark stars, specifically focusing on their mass and radius. Our discoveries demonstrate that both parameters react significantly to fluctuations in temperature and the intensity of the applied magnetic field. These theoretical outcomes align with the recent observational findings of squark stars under a strong magnetic field, as suggested by gravitational wave observations from the LIGO detector.
This study investigates the thermal and magnetic equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter, utilizing it to analyze the characteristics of spin-polarized quark stars at finite temperature. We consider both scenarios where the magnetic field is external and where it arises internally due to a non-vanishing chiral anomaly. In the first case, the equation of state softens, causing both the mass and radius of the stars to decrease as temperature rises. Conversely, in the second case, the equation of state hardens, leading to an increase in both mass and radius with temperature. However, in both cases, the influence of the magnetic field remains negligible at higher temperatures. These theoretical predictions align with the recently observed phenomenon that the radius of certain white dwarfs increases with temperature. Under a strong external magnetic field, our findings reveal that these stars exhibit the properties of conductive balls. This work contributes to the broader search for quark matter in the universe and informs the observational properties of compact stars in extreme environments, as evidenced by recent gravitational wave observations.
This study determines the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter (SPSQM) at non-zero temperatures within a strong magnetic field, specifically where the field intensity exceeds that generated by the star itself. The application of deep learning (DL) to extract meaningful data from 3D LiDAR has significantly enhanced place recognition, improving re-localization and loop-closure detection, especially under varying environmental conditions. We also investigated the impact of emotional valence on information diffusion and opinion, using Twitter data to test if content with positive vs. negative valence diffuses at different rates. Although many Kepler host stars are too dim for detailed follow-up, TESS has identified planets around nearby bright stars suitable for RV analysis. This paper introduces the TESS-Keck Survey (TKS), an RV initiative utilizing approximately 100 nights on the Keck/HIRES telescope to study TESS-discovered exoplanets. The survey's main goals include exploring the relationship between stellar properties and the composition of small planets, examining how system architectures vary with dynamical configurations or planet multiplicity, pinpointing prime targets for JWST atmospheric studies, and understanding how stellar evolution influences planetary systems. We present a fully automated target selection algorithm that identified 103 planets in 86 systems for the final TKS sample. The majority of TKS hosts are inactive, solar-like main-sequence stars with effective temperatures between 4500 K and 6000 K, spanning a broad range of metallicities. The selected sample features 71 small planets (Rp < 4 Re), 11 systems with multiple transiting candidates, 6 sub-day period planets, and 3 planets located in or near their host stars' habitable zones. This selection strategy will enable comparisons between measured planetary masses, densities, and eccentricities and predictions from population models. Our target list represents one of the largest and most precise samples of small, short-period planets currently available. This survey marks a vital step in connecting the discovery capabilities of TESS and the Keck Observatory and serves as a template for future analyses using data from TESS, Keck, and the JWST. Targets for the TKS are publicly accessible at http://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu.
Transit surveys conducted by Kepler, Kepler's K2 mode, SWARPer, and TESS have confirmed that small planets are abundant. While ground-based RV surveys have determined the masses of many Kepler hosts, the short durations and low signal-to-noise ratios of observations for small, faint stars have limited their ability to explore the full system properties of these planets. Conversely, TESS has identified many short-period planets around nearby, solar-type stars that are ideal for RV investigation, although most Kepler targets are unsuitable for such studies. This letter explores two potential strategies for performing RV follow-up on TESS exoplanets: utilizing all of TESS's observing time or dedicating only its second

This study examines online political discussions on Instagram through a network lens, specifically focusing on the formation of "co-commenter communities"—groups of users who frequently interact by commenting on the same posts and potentially steer ongoing conversations. We specifically target "salient co-interactions," which are interactions among co-commenters that occur significantly more often than would be expected by chance or independent behavior. Unlike casual interactions that happen frequently by accident, these salient interactions are crucial drivers of online discourse and information spread. Our research analyzes ten weeks of data centered on major elections in Brazil and Italy, tracking both politicians and celebrities. We characterize these co-commenter communities by examining their topological structure, the nature of the discussions within them, and how community composition and topics evolve over time. Our findings indicate that communities engaging with political topics are more deeply involved in debates, evidenced by longer comments and a higher frequency of emojis, hashtags, and negative language compared to other subjects. Furthermore, political discussion communities tend to be more dynamic; however, top commenters maintain their activity and membership within these groups over time. Finally, we observe significant temporal diversity in topics: while some attract fleeting attention, others centered on fundamental political issues remain consistently active. The study concludes by suggesting potential applications of this research for targeting misinformation. In terms of methodology, the paper details data collection techniques, describes platforms in terms of interest-based "followed-hashtag ensembles" and "common-interaction ensembles," and presents methods for analyzing topic focus via reverse IP addresses and reverse mention graphs. Additionally, various approaches for performing topological analysis are outlined. It is important to note that some data collection methods were employed before the COVID-19 pandemic, during a period of normal in-person activity. Various elements of the paper, including specific findings and methodologies, represent the views of the authors, which may differ from the perspectives of editors, publishers, or reviewers. astrophysics and exoplanet research. Within the M-dwarf sector, significant research has focused on developing empirical relations that utilize easily obtained observables to determine physical properties. While these relations often express the target quantity as a non-linear function of data, Bayesian modeling requires the inverse approach. This paper presents a novel Bayesian framework designed to simultaneously and self-consistently apply multiple empirical calibrations to fully characterize the mass, luminosity, radius, and effective temperature of field-age M-dwarfs. The framework introduces a new M-dwarf mass-radius relation exhibiting a 3.1% scatter at fixed mass. Additionally, we present the M-dwarf Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Sample (MUSS) and apply our methodology to derive consistent stellar parameters for these nearby low-mass stars, which were selected for their availability of ultraviolet spectroscopic data. These targets are primarily valuable as exoplanet hosts or benchmarks for multi-wavelength stellar activity studies. We utilize the field MUSS stars to define a low-mass main sequence in the solar neighborhood via Gaussian Process (GP) regression. These findings allow us to empirically identify a feature in the GP derivative at $\mathcal{M}_{b} = 0.337 \pm ^{0.013}_{0.026}$ $M_{\odot}$, marking the transition point where M-dwarfs shift from fully to partly convective interiors. Finally, we apply our revised mass-radius relation to exoplanet systems with transiting planets or derived host star radii, exploring how the uncertainties in the calibrations influence the derived planetary radii and densities for systems of all masses, including the超地球 (super-Earth) and mini-Neptune categories. We encourage future applications to other empirical relations and data sources, and we provide the fully Bayesian code used in this study as open source. We conclude by suggesting that this framework can be extended to other parts of the stellar population. We also highlight how it can assist in selecting targets for instruments like the UVEX all-sky survey and the Roman Space Telescope's Mega-Byte Depth Charge (MeTeOR) high-precision photometry program, which will enable the determination of planetary masses via radial velocity or astrometric methods and the direct measurement of planetary atmospheric compositions. Given that approximately 50% of M-dwarfs within 5 parsecs harbor planets, the proposed framework will play a crucial role in determining their properties and initiating the era of atmospheric studies for rocky planets around small

along the boundary of dual electromagnetic metasurfaces that maintain mirror reflection symmetry. Prior theoretical and experimental investigations have identified these waves in microwave and terahertz frequency ranges, demonstrating their emergence through a symmetric resistance transition from negative to positive values combined with uniform surface reactance. These waves exhibit tunable confinement, polarization dependent on direction, and singular field enhancement. This study introduces a graphene patch design that enables such waves to propagate within the optical domain. The proposed structure comprises a graphene metasurface situated on an epsilon-near-zero (ENZ) substrate. Although the approach accounts for both dual and homogeneous reactive impedances, the focus remains specifically on scenarios involving mirror symmetric resistance. Propagation characteristics, including frequency dependence and directionally tunable confinement, have been verified using finite element method (FEM) simulation. Additionally, these waves were observed experimentally using an ENZ substrate composed of an aluminum film and a graphene layer defined by electron beam lithography. Although optical observation confirmed the existence of surface waves, their uniqueness was validated via near-field scanning using an optical probe. Furthermore, the structure demonstrated frequency-tunable confinement and directional dependence regarding both confinement and polarization. This design offers significant potential for optical communication systems and sensing applications.

Although plasmonic surface waves possess sub-wavelength confinement, their propagation loss remains a constraint on miniaturizing photonic components. Recently, surface waves generated at interfaces with epsilon-near-zero (ENZ) materials were found to remain diffraction-limited. This paper reports surface wave propagation on a periodic structure made of an ENZ layer with varying thickness. These waves were detected using an optical probe in an experimental setup and verified by finite element method (FEM) simulations. The observed surface waves demonstrate both sub-wavelength confinement and the ability to propagate over distances exceeding the wavelength. These findings suggest that such surface waves are suitable for sensing applications and can utilize thick ENZ layers to achieve sub-wavelength confinement.

Surface waves propagating on a gold film exhibit group velocity dispersion (GVD) when the film thickness varies. In this work, we present both numerical simulations using the finite element method (FEM) and experimental validation of these waves on an aluminum film with adjustable thickness. Simulation results were confirmed through optical observation and near-field probing using an aperture probe in the visible spectrum. The aperture size functioned as a low-pass filter with a cutoff wavelength ($\lambda_c$) determined by the probe diameter $d$, expressed as $\lambda_c = d/2$. These findings open new avenues for designing compact devices capable of pulse compression or expansion

existing fine-grained complexity classifications for conjunctive queries currently exclude those containing self-joins. This paper investigates the impact of self-joins on enumeration complexity to extend current results into a general classification. We achieve this by analyzing the extension of two established dichotomies: one concerning linear delay and another regarding constant delay following linear preprocessing. Given the complexity of this inquiry, the paper adopts an example-driven approach to initiate the analysis. We demonstrate enumeration complexity results for various self-join scenarios to illustrate techniques that will be generalized. Specifically, we examine a family of queries representing the "basic" self-join case, which we define as Q_{\ell}, where \ell represents a non-negative integer. We establish both upper and lower bounds for these queries to aid the broader classification effort. Furthermore, we introduce the more complex "general" self-join category, comprising two distinct subsets. The first subset, labeled Q_{\scriptscriptstyle D}, includes queries featuring "diagonal" self-joins, while the second, labeled Q_{\scriptscriptstyle X}, contains queries with other types of self-joins. We provide complexity classifications for all queries within both the "basic" and "general" categories. It is important to note that our investigation is confined to instances with homogeneous relations. To support this classification, we define two novel structural characteristics: hyperlinearity and generalizability of linearization, which are further explored in our supporting lemmas and theorems. However, extending this work to problems with heterogeneous relations remains a topic for future research. Alongside the introductory examples, the queries discussed constitute a comprehensive classification. The findings presented in this paper enhance the overall understanding of database query evaluation complexity, specifically bridging the theoretical fields of database systems and fine-grained complexity. Along the way, we derive several related statement complexity results. To aid future research, the paper provides extensive code-heavy proofs, utilizing the {libFLIP} toolkit for clarity and both human and machine readability. We encourage adopting this tool for similar endeavors. To facilitate this, we have created an additional database query classification toolkit for fine-grained complexity, available at the following links: {https://orionzr.github.io/FLIPToolkit_for_Database_Queries/} and {https://github.com/OrionZR/FLIPToolkit_for_Database_Queries/}. We hope this resource supports future fine-grained complexity studies within the database domain. The provided links will be updated with any necessary changes

When restricted to the one-way model, these transducers characterize rational functions. Despite the robust characterization of regular functions by various finite-state devices, even the subclass of rational functions may include functions that are not computable by a Turing machine with infinite input. This paper introduces a decision procedure for the synthesis problem: given a regular function $f$ (specified by one of the aforementioned transducer models), determine if $f$ is computable, and if so, construct a Turing machine that computes it. A simplified variant, called next-generation reservoir computing (NGRC), further streamlines the process by eliminating many algorithmic hyperparameters to automatically identify high-performing traditional reservoir computers. This study examines a difficult scenario involving a dynamical system with multiple co-existing attractors and disparate time scales. By comparing NGRC and traditional reservoir computing using metrics that assess the geometry of both the true and predicted attractors, we analyzed a four-dimensional system. Results show that NGRC requires approximately 1.7 times less training data, needs $10^3$ times less warm-up time, involves fewer hyperparameters, and achieves roughly 100 times greater accuracy in predicting co-existing attractor characteristics than traditional reservoir computing. Additionally, the method successfully predicts the basin of attraction with high precision. These findings reinforce the superior learning capabilities of this new algorithm for modeling dynamical systems. The code is available at https://github.com/andres-rlz/NGRC.

for variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs (HJI) formulations—which yield the most permissive controller for state- and input-constrained problems subject to worst-case disturbances—we propose a second-order successive sweep algorithm to compute the zero sublevel sets of a standard reachability value functional. Assuming sufficient regularity and continuity of the HJI partial differential equation across the state space, we demonstrate that, under state feedback control against worst-case disturbances, this method enables the computation of the reachable state set within a specified verification time horizon. Numerical experiments illustrate the application of this technique to several state-constrained benchmark problems. Consequently, this work presents the first non-Eulerian technique designed to solve standard optimal control Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations. Furthermore, we anticipate that the principles established herein can be extended to nonstandard optimal control and differential game problems featuring convex cost and endpoint functionals, as well as those defined over compact, box-like state spaces. Finally, we expect that the results presented here will aid in addressing open challenges regarding state and input constrained differential games on compact state spaces, as well as in extending solutions to final state cost optimal control problems on such spaces. In all instances, the proposed method is expected to surpass the stateability and scalability limits currently imposed by Eulerian methods. The proof of the main theorem relies on a duality relationship linking the original viscosity solution of the HJI equation to the final state of an associated adjoint boundary value problem defined on a grid-point trajectory. We validate these findings through multiple numerical examples. The approach is supported by grid-apron scaling techniques and grid modification strategies of potential interest in other contexts. We conclude by providing implementations of the methods presented, which are available on GitHub. While recent advancements have enhanced their capacity to capture high-frequency details through periodic activations or positional encodings, these methods often sacrifice generalization, typically being optimized for only a single signal. We introduce a novel representation that generalizes across multiple instances while achieving state-of-the-art fidelity. Our approach employs a dual-MLP framework: a synthesis network maps a low-dimensional input (e.g., pixel coordinates) to an output domain (e.g., RGB values), while a modulation network translates a latent code specific to the target signal into parameters that adjust the synthesis network's periodic activations. Furthermore, we propose a local-functional representation that facilitates generalization by partitioning the signal's domain into a regular grid, where each tile is associated with a latent code. During testing, the signal is reconstructed with high fidelity by inferring or directly optimizing these latent codes. Consequently, our method produces generalizable functional representations for images, videos, and shapes, surpassing the reconstruction quality of previous works tailored to individual signals. Our code and results are publicly available.

While the visual categorization hypothesis attributes this continuum to the presence of animal-diagnostic features, the agency hypothesis suggests it reflects the perception of animals as social agents. In this study, we tested both theories using a stimulus set where visual categorizability and agency were dissociated, based on convolutional neural network representations and behavioral data. fMRI results revealed that visual categorizability and agency account for independent components of the animacy continuum in VTC; when modeled together, they fully explain the continuum. Furthermore, regions driven by visual categorizability were located posterior to those driven by agency. These findings indicate that multiple organizing principles, including agency, underpin the animacy continuum in VTC. We propose that, in natural viewing conditions, agency creates a distinct component of this continuum that was previously masked by the strong correlation between being an animal and being a potential agent in natural scenes. This research advances the agency hypothesis by providing the first empirical demonstration of its predictions through a novel, dissociating stimulus set. Additionally, we introduce a method for testing hypothesis-driven theories about neural representation structures in vision using behavioral data and CLIP-based measures of visual concept categorizability and other attributes. Finally, our work supports the broader view that theories of neural representation should be driven by behavioral data rather than relying solely on the properties of natural stimuli.

We present a systematic investigation into how different classes of representations for visual scene concepts are organized within the human visual system. Instead of focusing on a single proposed principle, we design experiments to contrast three class-level hypotheses: spatial topology, part-whole structure, and semantic network topology. To ensure a broad range of predictive outcomes, we employed the ALPINE framework to systematically generate image sets across 18 classification tasks derived from four distinct properties. Properties were selected to cover a wide spectrum of ecological validity and to facilitate strong, competing predictions from the various hypothesis classes. Results indicate that no single hypothesis class adequately explains how representations in the posterior-lateral VTC are organized; however, a hierarchy of these hypotheses does. Specifically, spatial topology is the dominant principle, accounted for by the other two in the anterior-medial VTC. Crucially, when spatial topology is controlled, the part-whole structure hypothesis emerges as the primary organizer for the remaining variance in anterior-medial VTC responses. To streamline the proofs for both the general claim and the optimized threshold, we define two standard lemmas at the conclusion.
