While applicable across all frequencies $\omega$, the method demonstrates particular efficiency in high-frequency scenarios. Built upon a time-domain framework, the approach comprises three stages: \emph{i)} generating an incoming plane wavelet with compact support along the propagation direction; \emph{ii)} resolving the scattering event in the time domain for this wavelet; and \emph{iii)} recovering the time-harmonic solution through a temporal Fourier transform of the time-domain result. A critical component is a front-tracking mesh adaptation algorithm employed in stage \emph{ii)}. By leveraging the localized nature of the wave front, this strategy significantly reduces the dependency of the required degrees of freedom on the frequency $\omega$ to achieve a specified accuracy. Furthermore, we introduce a specialized algorithm for the Fourier transform in stage \emph{iii)} that capitalizes on the reduced degrees of freedom inherent to the adapted meshes. Numerical tests validate the method's advantages and confirm its applicability to external source terms, including point sources and sound-soft scatterers. However, the achieved efficiency is constrained when trapping modes are present. Notably, the proposed approach is inherently parallelizable, making it well-suited for solving scattering problems involving high frequencies and three-dimensional material inhomogeneities. Keywords: Acoustic scattering, Finite Element Method, Direct and Adjoint Methods, Numerical Optimization, Fourier Transform.
This work benefits from discussions during the miniseminar on ``Computational Acoustics'' at the University of Bonn. The presented method should not be confused with techniques utilizing time-domain FEM followed by a Fourier transform, as those methods require additional degrees of freedom to ensure convergence to the time-harmonic solution.

one language into written text in another. Conventional cascaded systems, which combine Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Machine Translation (MT), often suffer from error propagation. While end-to-end architectures aim to eliminate this by utilizing a single system, they are hindered by a lack of training data. This study investigates zero-shot translation, a method that allows translation between unseen language pairs without requiring specific end-to-end ST data. Although effective in multilingual machine translation, zero-shot capabilities remain unexplored in the speech domain. Our approach constructs models trained exclusively on ASR and MT tasks that perform ST during inference. A primary obstacle is the significant disparity between audio and text representations, causing the models to learn these tasks differently. To address this, we develop two solutions: first, we train the models in an asymmetric manner, leveraging the larger capacity of the ASR component; second, we process the speech input through an ASR module before feeding the predicted text into the MT component. Experimental results demonstrate that these methods produce competitive zero-shot ST systems that do not rely on task-specific language pairs. Compared to baseline approaches, these models achieve improvements in both held-out test sets and real-world evaluations. Furthermore, they exhibit strong few-shot capabilities, successfully handling a limited number of additional language pairs. We release these models as a practical resource for handling unseen language pairs. The code is available at https://github.com/bartekd/ST-ZF and our findings at https://huggingface.co/spaces/bartekd/ST-ZF.

We determine that spherical multipoles are most effective for modeling the scattering of electromagnetic radiation, a finding demonstrated using an amorphous silicon sphere. Subsequently, these multipoles are applied to compute the optical forces exerted on semiconductor, dielectric, and metallic particles across a broad spectrum of wavelengths, spanning from the dipolar to the Mie regimes. Our results show that irreducible multipoles provide more accurate optical force predictions for semiconductors than the other two methods when the particle size is comparable to the wavelength, as do recent numerical approaches. In contrast, for particles much smaller than the wavelength, all three methods yield identical results, accurately predicting optical trapping in both the dipolar and Mie regimes. Finally, we examine the optical trapping of solar cells exposed to localized illumination, showing that spherical multipoles achieve an accuracy within 6% of the finite-element method for particles of any size. These multipoles are expected to be valuable in designing optical traps for micro- and nanoscale objects within real-world, complex scenarios. We anticipate that this work will stimulate future research into optical trapping using practical and sophisticated geometries. This study advances object modeling beyond the dipolar approximation, addressing a significant gap for particles of any size in both homogeneous and inhomogeneous media. To support these conclusions, the supplementary material provides analytic solutions for all test cases, including particle sizes ranging from dipolar to Mie regimes, as well as for dielectric, semiconductor, and metallic particles. Although designed for object sizes from dipolar to Mie and various material properties, these multipoles are particularly well-suited for semiconducting solar cells and nanodevices, accurately predicting optical forces in both small and large particle regimes while offering results that are 50 to 300 times faster than finite-element methods. Although the primary focus is on predicting optical forces, these multipoles are also applicable to other electromagnetic phenomena, including sensing, imaging, hyperthermal optical manipulation, and optical switching.

By extending the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw with the minimal dark sector, we establish a physical mechanism for neutrino oscillation lengths: the atmospheric mass scale originates from tree-level seesaw dynamics, whereas the solar scale emerges radiatively through mediation by the dark sector. Complex geometries usually necessitate unstructured mesh discretization, making direct potential evaluation via quadrature computationally expensive. This paper introduces a straightforward, high-order algorithm for calculating Newtonian potentials by leveraging Green's third identity to convert volume integrals into boundary integrals, which are then processed using the Helsing-Ojala method. Consequently, the time required for traditionally costly near-field and self-interaction calculations on unstructured meshes becomes comparable to that of far-field interactions computed via the Fast Multipole Method (FMM). A central component of this algorithm is the high-order 2-D monomial approximation of the function's harmonic extension into the mesh volume, which is computed directly—bypassing the need for often numerically unstable tri-diagonal matrix solvers. By relying solely on matrix-vector multiplications, the algorithm is particularly well-suited for parallel execution on GPU architectures. Despite this parallelization potential, the algorithm's efficiency in serial execution is also demonstrated. Test cases involving a electrostatics problem on a bounded mesh and a self-gravitating cloud confirm the method's high accuracy and speed. Notably, these tests also validate the direct high-order harmonic monomial calculation's superior performance compared to the conventional approach of solving for coefficients via a mesh's adjacency matrix. Finally, the algorithm's parallelization is tested using both the FMM and parallelization through multi-nodal expansion.

Calculating Newtonian potentials via direct integration on an unstructured mesh is significantly slower than using fast methods like the Fast Multipole Method (FMM), especially for near-field interactions. This discrepancy is even more pronounced when solving Poisson's equation for a closed volume, as there is no boundary term to reduce the integral's dimensionality. This paper presents a high-order algorithm for evaluating Newtonian potentials throughout a volume by combining the High-Order Fast Directivity (HOFD) method with the Divergence Theorem. Unlike traditional approaches that sum expansion coefficients, this work utilizes a recursive formulation based on the addition theorem for spherical harmonics, enabling parallel computation on a GPU. Additionally, the paper addresses the specific case of constant density (up to a smooth function) using a particularly efficient technique. Testing on a sphere and a "Riemann" shape (a room with an internal obstacle) reveals a speedup of up to 28 times compared to the classical fully parallelized FMM.
